utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I first verify that the equipment is working? Everyone in the courtroom who cannot understand me should have their earphones on. Can everyone who is wearing earphones in the courtroom hear me in a language they understand? Mr. Tadic? Can you hear me in a language you understand? Fine, thank you. May I have the appearances for the Prosecutor, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Miss Hollis, Mr. Tieger and Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. May I have the appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Michail Wladimiroff. I am advocate at the Bar of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands and I am counsel for the Defence. On my left side is Alphons Orie who is also an advocate at the Bar of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands, co-counsel for the Defence; on my right side, Steven Kay, barrister of the Bar of England and Wales, co-counsel for the Defence and on my far left side is Sylvia de Bertodano, also a barrister of the Bar of England and Wales assisting the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we have the opening statements I need to discuss with you lawyers this morning various motions that we considered at the pretrial conference on Friday. We need to announce our rulings on those motions. The first motion is the Prosecutor's motion to compel disclosure of statements of witnesses of the Defence. That motion is denied. The second motion is the Prosecutor's motion for protective measures for witness P. That motion is granted. The next motion is the Defence's motion for summons and for protective measures. That has several parts to it. First, the request that the Trial Chamber summons witnesses will be granted. The request for safe conduct is granted. The request for video conference testimony is granted in part and denied in part. The request for confidentiality of certain witnesses is granted in part and denied in part. The request for anonymity of witnesses is denied. As to each of those last parts of the motions, that is the motion, the request for video conference, the request for confidentiality and the request for anonymity, leave will be granted to the Defence to supplement its declarations that you submitted in support of those motions by May 31st. The last motion that we discussed at the pretrial conference was the motion of the Prosecutor to withdraw counts 2 through 4. I will address that in a moment. The final matter that we discussed at the pretrial conference related to the request of the Prosecutor and the request of the Defence that the Trial Chamber make a ruling, a preliminary ruling, on various matters that you had addressed in your pretrial briefs. At the pretrial conference on Friday, we advised the parties, at least in four areas, that we could give you some direction on and it was our belief that giving you direction in those four areas was sufficient. Let me just repeat what I told you then. First, the Trial Chamber has determined that no information that relates exclusively to the sentencing should be presented by the witnesses during the trial as to guilt or innocence. We directed you to Rule 100 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. What we are saying is that we understand the position of the Prosecutor and we understand the position of the Defence. If you have, however, a witness who testifies, a witness may testify as to guilt or innocence, but if the witness's testimony is also solely directed towards matters that we should consider as a part of sentencing, we consider that we should hear that pursuant to the terms of Rule 100. Was it Mr. Kay or was it Mr. Wladimiroff, no, I think it was Mr. Orie, yes, who suggested, that is fine, we have made that ruling, but how we will make that determination will be something else. You are probably correct, Mr. Orie, but that is our ruling in that regard. The second ruling had to do with a request of the Prosecutor that the Trial Chamber make findings as to the guilt of the accused with respect to a crime that was not specifically charged in the indictment. The Trial Chamber declines to make such a ruling. We do not consider that it is appropriate to find that the accused is guilty of a crime that is not specifically charged as such in the indictment. The third ruling related to the responsibility of the parties to give evidence as to the character of the conflict. The Trial Chamber does want to hear evidence as to the character of the conflict. I think the Defence had taken the position that the Appeals Chamber had found that the conflict was internal; the Prosecutor had taken the position that the Appeals Chamber had found that the conflict was international although, perhaps, there was some confusion about that. The Trial Chamber has determined that it does wish to hear testimony regarding the character of the conflict. Finally, the Trial Chamber determined that it was necessary to offer evidence, that it was necessary for the Prosecutor to offer evidence, that the crimes charged in the indictment were committed in the context of an armed conflict. We consider that that is a burden that the Prosecutor must bear. We then discussed -- I suppose we will discuss again -- the request of the Prosecutor, joined in by the Defence, that the Trial Chamber make certain rulings regarding the elements of the offence. We consider that the rulings that we have made thus far are sufficient to give you direction as far as the eliciting of evidence is concerned. We received again this morning the request of the Prosecutor and the Defence. The Trial Chamber does not consider that it is appropriate for us at this time to basically formulate an international criminal code; instead, we think it is our responsibility to hear the evidence and to interpret and apply the terms of the Statute of the International Tribunal. So, that is as far as we will go with respect to your request. We think that we have given you what is necessary to guide you in the offering of evidence and that, I hope, ends that matter, although I certainly understand your position. Are there any other preliminary matters, other than the Prosecutor's motion to withdraw counts 2 through 4, that we need to discuss before I hear the readiness of the parties and the presentation of the opening statements? Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not from the Defence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. Is the Prosecutor ready to proceed to trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Prosecution is ready, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Is the Defence ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So is the Defence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann, we had determined at the pretrial conference on Friday that the Prosecutor would submit its motion to withdraw counts 2 through 4 of the indictment before you presented your opening statements. Are you ready to make that presentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. The Prosecution seeks to withdraw counts 2 through 4 of the indictment on a without prejudice basis. In all other respects, your Honour, we rely upon the motion filed and the submissions that I made at the pretrial conference on Friday.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we rely on the response we have given at the pretrial conference and we refer to our position in that response.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. We interpreted that as being no objection to either the withdrawal or, perhaps, treatment of the motion as an amendment without prejudice, although subject, as I recall, to your opportunity to present at a later date, should the Prosecutor seek to indict Mr. Tadic once again with respect to these charges, any defences that you have at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is correct, indeed, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, the Prosecutor has filed that motion with the Registry prior to the commencement of trial. I understand from the Registrar that it is more appropriate for that motion to be withdrawn as having been filed prior to the commencement of trial and now resubmitted now the trial has commenced. So, we will consider that that motion has been withdrawn from the Registry and resubmitted as a trial amendment, or as a motion to withdraw under either Rules 50 or 51 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Is that the correct procedure? The Registrar will tell me? Is that acceptable? MRS. DE SAMPAYO: It seems acceptable to me, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. The Trial Chamber then will consider the motion to withdraw counts 2 through 4 as being submitted as an amendment to the indictment pursuant to Rule 50 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, that being simply a dropping of counts 2 through 4. There is no need to postpone the trial. Those counts, counts 2 through 4, charged the accused with forcible sexual intercourse in violation of Articles 2(B), 3 and 5 of the Statute of the International Tribunal and Article 3.1.3 of the Geneva Convention of 1949. Is that correct, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are those the counts that you wish to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Or, rather, I suppose we decided that we will treat it as a trial amendment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Amendment, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. That motion then will be granted. Before hearing opening statements from the parties, the Chamber thought that it was appropriate to make some very brief introductory remarks to, at least, put this trial in context as we see it. This is the beginning of the first trial before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia; an International Tribunal specially created by the United Nations to try persons charged with serious violations of international humanitarian law in the former Yugoslavia. As such an occasion, this has certain historic dimensions. Nevertheless, we should all remember first and foremost that this is a criminal trial of an accused who a little over one year ago appeared before this Chamber and entered a plea of not guilty. Under any system of justice, he is entitled to a fair trial and to ensure that he receives one is our paramount purpose for being here. The lawyers appearing on each side of this case come from different legal systems, as do each of we three Judges, but we all agree on one premise and that is that the rule of law must be upheld and that fairness is a cornerstone of the process of affording justice. In conducting the trial, the Judges will be guided by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that the Tribunal has adopted. As you lawyers know, we have approximately 125 Rules of Procedure and Evidence, but we only have 10 rules of evidence that will guide the conduct of the trial and the receipt of evidence, compared with the dozens of often times hypertechnical rules of other legal systems. We have no rule of hearsay, for example, and Rule 89(C) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence provides that a Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value, and Rule 89(B) of our Rules of Evidence requires that the Trial Chamber apply the rules of evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law. In this context, we, Judges, will be tryers of fact and we will apply the law to our findings. The extensive pretrial discussions that have taken place, the many pretrial motions that have been dealt with, have all been aimed at ensuring that this first trial will be conducted as fairly and as expeditiously as possible with justice being both done and being seen to be done. Regardless of all of the apparent trappings of today, that is our sole raison d'etre. We will be working together on this trial, whether at the Bench or at the Bar tables for many weeks. We encourage you to be at ease to the extent that it is possible under all of these circumstances, and we ask that counsel discharge their responsibilities in a professional manner. As we have previously indicated in an order that has been entered by the Trial Chamber, the trial will be conducted from 10 a.m. until 1 p.m., and then 2.30 to 5.30 p.m. with a 15 minute break in the morning and a 15 minute break in the afternoon. We plan to hear evidence from Tuesday through Friday of every week except this month which has a very, very different schedule for many reasons. On Mondays, this courtroom (which is the only courtroom that this Tribunal has) will be set aside for other matters to be considered by the Trial Chamber and as well as the other Trial Chamber. The Prosecution may proceed with its opening remarks. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. As your Honour has observed, the opening of the first case before the Tribunal is an historic occasion but it is also a solemn one. The duty of any criminal court is onerous, but the duty imposed on this Tribunal is a heavy burden indeed. This Tribunal has been created not only to administer justice in respect of the accused that stands before you, but there is an expectation that in so doing you will contribute to a lasting peace in the country that was once Yugoslavia. The human tragedy that has occurred in the former Yugoslavia since 1991 is of major proportions. When dealing with violations of international humanitarian law, we are not only looking to the actions of individuals, but to the involvements of the authorities of the state as well. Through this trial we will embark upon an examination of events of unspeakable horror. What man has done to man in the cause of nationalism, or ethnic hegemony in the former Yugoslavia, strains the most agile of human reasoning. The evidence of the Prosecution will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused Dusko Tadic committed the crimes with which he has been charged, and that it was pursuant to a widespread or systematic attack against the non-Serb population of the opstina Prijedor in order to achieve the goal of the Serbian state, that it would remain as part of what later became the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. When an individual commits a crime, the state stands as the bastion of justice, but when the state commits the crime only the community of nations can protect the individual, otherwise evil has no boundary. The witnesses that will come before you are often bewildered and sometimes angry about the tragic and undeserved fate that has befallen them. The absolute terror to which they have been subjected in those black days of 1992 and the passage of time since then may have had some effect on their ability to relate all the details of their experiences, but their sincerity and their veracity regarding the crimes they describe and the responsibility of the accused for those crimes are, in our submission, beyond question. While this trial is primarily concerned with what occurred between the accused and the victims of his crimes, it is also concerned with the tragic destruction of that once proud and beautiful country of Yugoslavia. To have some understanding of the nature of the conflict, to have some understanding of the people of Yugoslavia and their ethnic composition, to have some understanding of why one ethnic group would want to so cruelly turn upon another with the intent of bringing about their destruction, to have some understanding of the targeted victims of these crimes, then it is necessary to have some understanding of what was Yugoslavia. To this end, we will bring evidence about Yugoslavia itself. The evidence will show that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia consisted of six states: Bosnia Herzegovina; Croatia; Macedonia; Montenegro; Serbia and Slovenia. The ethnic composition of the Federation in descending order of population size were Serbians; Croatians; Muslims; Slovenes; Macedonians; Albanians; Hungarians and others. The major language is Serbo-Croat which is a single orthography containing a Latin and Cyrillic script. The major religions are Roman Catholicism; Eastern Orthodoxy and Islam. If your Honours please, I will now display on the monitors a map given the number 2-1 which, in due course, will be tendered in the course of the evidence. If your Honours please, this map when displayed -- I think it should come on the computer monitor -- will show Yugoslavia in its entirety consisting of the six states of Macedonia, Serbia, Montenegro Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, Slovenia and the two independent provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo. Your Honours, the bringing of Yugoslavia into a federation of states was the realisation of a dream, but it also was an uneasy attempt to embrace the complicated mixture of diverse peoples, cultures, historic and religious traditions and geography. This diversity was especially prominent in Bosnia where Catholic, Orthodox and Muslim populations co-existed until the country was enveloped by political tension and armed hostilities in the early part of the 1990s. Sadly, this tragic land has had a long history of bloody conflict which has, no doubt, had some influence on the national outlook. Although the peoples of Yugoslavia, especially Bosnia, are no different to any other peoples of the world in merely wanting to live in peace, the history of bloodshed inhibits their confidence in achieving and maintaining a peaceful nation where ethnic harmony and security is assured. The tension between the Yugoslav ideal of one people and the ethnic divisions promoted by the nationalist interests of the various republics waxed and waned throughout the 20th century. By 1974, the then new constitution ensured that there would be a tight unifying control over the various republics but that such control would be decentralised and exercised at the republic level. The investing of greater power in the respective republics worked during the life of Tito, mainly because he was able to exercise sufficient control over the various factions so as to stop them from breaking apart. After Tito's death in 1980, things deteriorated rapidly and the rotating presidency not only failed to work but actually contributed to the final collapse of the Federation. The Serbian perspective was nurtured by their folklore as victims throughout history, including what happened to them during the Second World War at the hands of the Nazi backed Ustasha, which was to be suspicious of and to try to achieve hegemony over the other states of Yugoslavia. In 1990, there was held the first democratic elections in the Republics since the Second World War. In Slovenia, the former communists in coalition with the four opposition parties were elected. In Croatia, the leader of the Croatian Democratic Union, Franjo Tudjman, became the President. In Bosnia, the major political parties were constituted along nationalistic lines. The Muslim SDA or the Party of Democratic Action gained about one-third of the seats in the Parliament with the Serbian Democratic Party (SDS) gaining 30 per cent; the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) about 20 per cent and 13 per cent of the seats were taken by non-nationalistic parties. Alija Izetbegovic, the SDA leader, was elected by a seven member presidency as the President. In Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic became the President of the Republic of Serbia. The results of these elections demonstrated a deep division along ethnic lines. The fragile state of the Federal economy, the growing forces of nationalism and the quest for independent sovereignty of each of the republics with the possible exception of Bosnia meant that the life of the Federation was limited. On 23rd December 1990, Slovenia held a referendum on independence. On 15th May 1991, Serbia blocked what should have been an automatic procedure and prevented Croatia from having its turn on the collective Presidency, thus leaving Yugoslavia without a head of State. Thus, the Federal system could no longer work. On 19th May 1991, Croatia held a referendum on independence. On 25th June 1991, Slovenia issued declarations of independence. The break-up of the Federation opened the question of what was to happen to the military forces. The armed forces of the Republic of Yugoslavia, referred to as the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, comprised two elements. The first level was the Yugoslav People's Army, referred to as the "JNA"; the second level was the Territorial Defence Forces, the "TO", which was a Republican based force derived from the traditions of the partisans in guerrilla warfare during the Second World War. The Federal Secretariat for the People's Defence directed the JNA. The Secretariat for the People's Defence in each of the Republics was responsible for the Territorial Defence. The philosophy behind this two-tiered structure of defence forces was that the JNA was to be the first echelon of the defence to resist initial attack and to carry out holding operations while the TO mobilised. It was always assumed that both tiers of the armed forces would operate together, which they might well have done had Yugoslavia been attacked from outside, but what was not realised was that in the event of a civil war the Territorial Defence aligned along nationalist ethnic lines would be potentially in conflict with the Federal JNA. Initially, the JNA was a true reflection of its federal mandate and was composed in its command structure of a representative level of personnel from each of the republics. But with the disintegration of the republic in the late 1980s and early 1990s, the republic's representation began to decline in favour of an increasing Serbian dominance, such that by March 1992 the Serb component of the officer corps of the JNA had risen to in excess of 90 per cent. Then when the JNA went to war to protect the break up of the Federation, it did so not as the Yugoslav Federal army but as the de facto Army of Serbia. Immediately after the Slovenian and Croatian declarations of independence, the JNA together with other Serb forces responded with armed force. The Slovenian TO, Territorial Defence, proved effective against the JNA. The European Community offered to mediate; a move which surprised the JNA, which then feared Western military intervention. Accordingly, it abandoned its fight against Slovenia and concentrated on Croatia where it was perceived that Serb military populations were potentially under threat. It soon became apparent that the quest for Croatian sovereignty would prevail in the face of Serb dominated Yugoslav federation. Accordingly, the JNA took steps to preserve Serbian interests in Bosnia. In 1990, the JNA ordered all TOs in Yugoslavia to turn over their weapon stocks. The fact that Slovenia refused to do so was the key to their successful defence. In Croatia, most of the units also turned in their weapons, which helps explain Croatia's initial difficulties in its defence. When Bosnia made it clear of its intention to seek independence, the JNA began to redistribute the arms to the Bosnia Serb population. With increasing tensions in Bosnia, in December 1991 Bosnia applied to the European Community for diplomatic recognition. Bosnian Serbs then set up their own Serbian Autonomous Region in Bosnia. In March 1992 a referendum was held to determine the future of Bosnia's membership of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Bosnian Serb leaders boycotted the referendum. Despite the boycott, 63 per cent participated in the vote, 90 per cent voted for independence. On 6th March 1992, President Izetbegovic declared Bosnia's independence and called for international recognition. Recognition came from some quarters as early as 6th April 1992. On 7th April 1992, Bosnian-Serb leaders declared what was to become the independent Republika Srpska. Following these moves a brutal war then ensued. Between March and May 1992, the JNA aided by the Territorial Defence units, police forces and various paramilitary groups, such as those led by Seselj and Arkan, engaged in a series of apparently co-ordinated attacks and takeovers to secure the main entry points into Bosnia as well as major communications and logistics lines, for example, Bosanki Brod on 27th March 1992; at Derventa and Bijelina on 2nd April 1992; at Kupres on 4th April 1992; at Foca and Zvornik on 8th April 1992; at Visegrad on 13th April 1992; at Bosanki Samac on 17th April 1992; at Vlasenica on 18th April 1992; at Brcko and Prijedor on 30th April 1992. If your Honours please, if the technician is good enough to put upon the screens, map 2-20.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I presume these will be identified and then offered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tendered in the course of evidence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is map 2 of -- I did not hear the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 2-20. Your Honour, that is a computer reference, your Honour. Your Honours can see some of the towns mentioned in highlight there on that map showing Brcko, Bosanski Samac, Prijedor and Vlasenica. One can see the surrounding republics of Serbia, Montenegro and then to the left is Croatia. As the attacks progressed, the combined Serb forces conducted a campaign of terror to drive out the non-Serbs and those "disloyal" Serbs from the occupied areas. The label given to this practice was coined by the Serbian extreme nationalist leader, Voislav Seselj, in 1991/92 as "ethnic cleansing". On 19th May 1992, in an apparent effort to distance itself from the Bosnian conflict, Belgrade ordered the division of the JNA in Bosnia to the Serbian Army in Bosnia (later to be known as the army of the Republika Srpska, or the VRS) and the Army of Yugoslavia, the VJ. However, the VRS, the Republic of Srpska Army, was left largely intact, with significant military equipment, including tanks, heavy artillery and munitions. The only significant difference was that the new VRS, the Republic of Srprska Army, was staffed by Serbians from Bosnia and the non-Bosnian Serbs soldiers from Serbia were allowed to return to the rump Yugoslavia. However, despite the public statements, officers were not encouraged to leave, but rather to stay and, as a result, the officers of the VRS, the Republika Srpska Army, were in large measure the same ones who had run the same units for the JNA. In addition, the direct support of the VRS by the JNA and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia continued, including the payment of salaries to officers. The Republika Srpska Army received also direct logistical support at all levels. Accordingly, there was still significant involvement in the Bosnian conflict by Belgrade after the division of the army in May 1992. Through the spring offensive of April/May 1992 by the JNA, with Territorial Defence units and police forces and pro-Serb paramilitary groups was planned, a systematic and co-ordinated attack. Preparations for the offensive started in late 1991. The JNA supplied paramilitary groups and Bosnian-Serb volunteers with weapons and munitions and proceeded to disarm the non-Serb population. In those areas where the Serbs were not in control of the local administrations, including the police, every effort was made to undermine their authority. In most of the occupied cities, the Serbs set up "crisis Headquarters" which took over the control of the local government including the Territorial Defence. In those places where this occurred, the Serb population received advance notice -- the Bosnian-Serb population received advance notice of what was about to occur. In those cities where there was to be a Serbian attack either by the JNA, paramilitary groups or both, a significant proportion of the Bosnian-Serb population was evacuated before the attack commenced. This pattern repeated itself in a consistent manner all over Bosnia. Many Muslims tried to negotiate a resolution in the hope of avoiding violence. As a consequence, the Muslims did little in preparation for the Serbian attack. The military operations by the JNA and the pro-Serb paramilitary groups followed in a consistent pattern. Excessive amounts of artillery was used in the initial stages to shell non-Serb neighbourhoods in order to discourage resistance, non-Serbs were expelled from the area and where resistance occurred it was ruthlessly crushed. The artillery attack by the JNA was usually co-ordinated with street fighting by the paramilitary groups who were assisted by Serb irregulars in street fighting and the rounding up of the non-Serbs of the district. The paramilitary group operated right across Bosnia. The rounding-up of the non-Bosnian-Serb population was a systematic and thorough operation, with the paramilitary groups relying on local information and identification of the non-Serbs by the local irregulars. Once the non-Serb population had been collected together, they were then sorted: Women, children and elderly men were separated from the men of military age, although at times and in some places all men were separated from the women and children, making the women much more vulnerable to rape and mistreatment. Terror tactics such as killings, rapes and tortures, were used apparently condoned by the paramilitary commanders. The JNA, and the paramilitary commanders during the sweeps through non-Serb neighbourhoods participated in this activity. The terror served to intimidate and discourage resistance and to compel non-Serbs to leave the area. Following the military attack, the crisis headquarters took over. These crisis headquarters worked closely with the military and usually had military personnel represented on the committees. They established curfews, restricted travel, dismissed non-Serbs from their jobs and continued the process of identification and identification of the non-Serb population. During the attacks or following non-Serb cultural and religious symbols such as mosques and Catholic churches were destroyed. Non-Serb businesses and houses were also systematically destroyed. In order to house the non-Serb population that had been identified and collected by the military or crisis headquarters, the Serbs established a series of camps throughout Bosnia. Conditions in the camps were for the most part appalling. The camps were also classified according to use. Some camps were used for the women and the children where rapes and mistreatment were common. Other camps were used as torture centres where men usually (but not always men) were savagely beaten and killed. The brutal conditions in these camps were in furtherance of a campaign of terror designated to persuade non-Serbs to abandon their homes and leave the area, or for them to be otherwise destroyed. The events of this case are concentrated in the region of north-west Bosnia known as Opstina Prijedor. The main city in Prijedor bears the same name as the Opstina. But other significant towns to feature in the evidence are Kozarac, Trnopolje, Omarska, Hambarine, Kozarusa, Kamincani, Jaskici and Sivci, just to mention a few. If your Honour pleases, I might ask the technician to put on the screen map 2-21 which places Prijedor Opstina surrounded by the Opstinas of Sanski Most, Banja Luka, Bosanski Novi and the others that one can see on the screen. Your Honours, Prijedor was significant to the Serbs because it is strategically placed in a corridor that links the Serb dominated area in the Croatian Krajina to the west, with Serbia and Montenegro to the east and the south. The Krajina Serbs have lived on either side of the Bosnian border with Croatia for generations. During World War II, this was the heart of the Ustasha territory where the Serbs were subjected to the appalling torture. Before the war, the population of Prijedor was almost evenly divided between Muslims and Serbs. But by June 1993, of the nearly 50,000 Muslims living in the Opstina before the war, all but about 1,000 had either left or been killed. Although election results in 1990 suggested that the local administration should be shared by Muslims and the Serbs, Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs who had previously dominated the local administration resisted the Muslims taking control of local institutions. By late 1991, the Serbs of Prijedor were instructed by the central leadership of the Serbian Nationalist Party, the SDS, to prepare for the taking over of all local institutions. The Serbian crisis headquarters of Prijedor was in place immediately following the military takeover of the region by the JNA on 30th April 1992. The military situation in the Prijedor region was dominated by the 5th Corps of the JNA, whose headquarters was in Banja Luka. After 19th May 1992, the 5th Corps was designated the 1st Krajina Corps of the Republic of Srpska Army, but it had the exact same Commanding General and officer Corps. It was the 5th Corps which ordered the deployment of artillery and troops on the hills surrounding the Kozarac area, from where they looked down on the population below. Television signals to Prijedor were mostly transmitted from a tower on Kozara mountain. However, in 1992, Prijedor residents found that they were no longer able to receive television from Sarajevo or from Zagreb, but only from Belgrade. Belgrade television broadcast anti-Muslim and anti-Croat propaganda which escalated in intensity, repeatedly accusing non-Serb extremists for plotting against the Serbs. On the night of 30th April 1992, Serb forces seized the town of Prijedor. There was no resistance. Non-Serb police surrendered their arms. Serbs took over control of the civilian administration and renamed the Opstina as "Srpska Opstina Prijedor". Over the next few weeks, radio Prijedor repeatedly broadcast demands for the non-Serbs to surrender their arms. Travel for non-Serbs was curtailed, and they were dismissed from their jobs. Communications from Muslim villages were cut off. On 22nd May 1992, during a confrontation at a Muslim checkpoint in Hambarine, a predominantly Muslim village, two Serbs were killed. The next day Serb forces launched an attack with artillery and tanks. The village was destroyed and the population fled. In about the centre of the Opstina Prijedor is the town of Kozarac. There was nothing in particular to distinguish this town from a multitude of other towns in Bosnia, except that the majority of the population were Muslim. When the war came to Kozarac, it came with particular ferocity. The usual hallmarks of the attack were present in Kozarac, as they were right across Bosnia, where the JNA aided by the paramilitary and irregular forces attacked the non-Serb areas. The checkpoints were established, freedom of movement was restricted. A false pretext was raised to justify the Serb attack, and the Muslims were generally ill-prepared for war. When the JNA surrounded the area of Kozarac the Serb military commander, Radmilo Zeljaja, demanded that the local Muslims pledge loyalty to the Serb authority or face annihilation. The town of Kozarac itself was a community of approximately 4,000 persons. Kozarac was predominantly a Muslim village and of the population of 4,000 about 3,700 of them are Muslim. Kozarac was a centre for the surrounding villages of Trnopolje, Kozarusa and Kamincani. The town had a school, a medical clinic, a police station, a number of mosques, one orthodox church, an ambulance station, a number of restaurants, hairdressers, mixed businesses and the like. The major industry in the area was timber, with a timber mill located on the outskirts of the town. In the main street of the town, there were a number of bars and cafes where the local community would regularly gather in order to socialise. Up until the 1990s, the various ethnic groups socialised freely with one another but, as the clouds of conflict began to gather, signs of ethnic tension became more and more visible in Kozarac. One of the bars in the centre of the town diagonally opposite the school on Marsala Tita Street was called the "Nipon" cafe. This bar was owned by the accused, Dusko Tadic, also referred to as Dule or Dusan Tadic. Tadic was born in Kozarac on 1st April 1995 (sic), the son of a decorated Serbian World War II veteran, Ostoje Tadic, and his wife, Staka. As a young man and after completion of his high school studies, Dusko Tadic did his military service. He then went back to Kozarac where he was married. Tadic had an enduring interest in Karate, where he excelled, gaining the level of black belt. He set up a Karate school which failed. He taught Karate at the local school in Kozarac across from his house. He had a number of friends who shared his interest in Karate, several of these friends were Muslims. As young men, they would often measure the worth of their prowess in terms of their ability at Karate. The cafe-bar was set up at the bottom of his house. The accused Tadic appeared to get on well with the Muslim population and among his close associates was one Emir Karabasic. However, as the 1992 war approached, all this was to change. Tadic was to exhibit staunch Serb nationalist sentiments and progressively adopt anti-Muslim attitudes. He also became involved in politics, especially with the emergence of the Serb Nationalist Party, the SDS. In view of his known Serb nationalist preferences, Tadic was relied upon by the Serb forces during the 1992 spring offensive directed against Kozarac. Just prior to the attack on Kozarac on 24th May 1992, in full knowledge of what was about to happen, Tadic evacuated his family from Kozarac so as to take them out of the line of fire of the advancing Serb Army. Tadic was willingly used by the advancing Serb forces as an important source of intelligence and as a person capable of identifying local Muslims, Croats and other persons disloyal to the Serb nationalist cause. In all the traditions of the "fifth column", he skillfully performed his task. During 1992, he rose from relative obscurity to a person of influence in the Kozarac area as a result of his new position in the SDS. No doubt, his local knowledge and known reliability was of considerable utility to the Serbian military and civilian administrations. While the local community in Kozarac, mostly Muslims, were desperately trying to negotiate a peaceful settlement of the crisis, thereby avoiding bloodshed and destruction, the Serbs attacked. Tadic, to the eleventh hour, endeavoured to present himself as a friend of the Muslims of Kozarac. He attended negotiations between the Serbs and the Muslims pretending to support the Muslims, but knowing full well at all times that, in reality, he had not the slightest intention of advancing their cause. The shelling of Kozarac and the surrounding villages commenced on 24th May 1992 and continued for two days. Tadic was now able to emerge from his undercover role. Forewarned and according to plan, Tadic as an aid to the Serb military surrounding the town, assisted the artillery attack on Kozarac by firing flares in the air at night over his preselected targets. On 27th May 1992, the shelling of Kozarac ceased. Defenceless and unable to negotiate a cease-fire, the terrified towns folk, mostly Muslims and non-Serbs, desperately clinging to their white flags emerged in their thousands from their hiding places, in basements, under rubble and in creek beds. These people were not soldiers, they were not armed, they were for the most part civilians, including women, children and the elderly. They were the innocent citizens of this area. Serbian soldiers and local armed citizens, including Tadic, who by now had armed himself with an automatic weapon, ordered these unfortunate people to form into columns, to remain silent and to keep their heads bowed. They were then marched through Kozarac, as the trophy of war, to the taunts and curses of the Serb on-lookers. Some of the Muslims and non-Serbs were pulled out from the line and beaten or killed. The bodies of the dead were left beside the roads as the column marched by. Mothers and fathers watched in horror as their military aged sons were pulled out from the column and shot before their very eyes. Marching in this column was Ismet and Ekrem Karabasic, their brother's son, Seido Karabasic, 21 years of age, and Redo Foric. None of these men were armed. They were of no military threat whatsoever. They were all Muslims. They were with members of their family. They all seemed to have been known by either Tadic or his accomplice there that day, Goran Borovnica. Borovnica was a close friend of Tadic before the war, and continued as a friend during the course of the war. On this particular day, Tadic and Borovnica were acting in concert. As the column approached the centre of Kozarac in the vicinity of a small bar which served grilled meat, Borovnica and Tadic were calling out the names of the people in the column and ordering them to leave the column. Nearby was a pile of corpses dressed in civilian clothing, approximately 20 in number. Tadic and Borovnica then called out Ismet, Ekrem and Seido Karabasic and Redo Foric. These men were then forced to stand against the wall, facing the wall, with their hands raised above their heads. They were then shot with bursts of fire from automatic weapons. For the non-Serbs of Kozarac, their families were torn apart. Loved ones were taken away and never seen again. Properties were destroyed and hopes and dreams were shattered. A reign of unimaginable terror had begun. Men were segregated from women and children. Some of the men were taken to the Prijedor police station where many of them were beaten. For a large number of these men this was the beginning of a sustained campaign of beatings. Most of the men ended up in camps in Omarska or Keraterm. The others, including women and children, were sent to Trnopolje. Conditions at all the camps were appalling, but Omarska and Keraterm stand out as the camps where the most horrific of atrocities were committed. There was evidence of co-ordination between these camps. The three main camps in the Opstina, as I said, were Omarska, which was a former mining complex, Keraterm, a former ceramics factory, and Trnopolje, a former school. The towns where the camps are located are indicated on a map that I might ask now be shown on the screen, 2-22. Your Honours can see there the towns of Kozarac, Trnopolje and down to the bottom right-hand corner of the screen, Omarska. The camp at Keraterm is, in fact, part of the town of Prijedor and is not referred to on the map. But one can see that these camps are all in close proximity to one another and all in close proximity to the town of Prijedor. Omarska held those who were prominent in the Muslim society, intellectuals, politicians and businessmen. A lesser number were held at this camp than at the other camps such as Trnopolje. Prisoners at Omarska were systematically murdered, beaten or otherwise subjected to terrible degradation. The camp at Keraterm was located, as I said, in what was previously a ceramics factory on the outskirts of the city of Prijedor. The camp consisted of one large building being divided into several separate rooms. There was no heating or cooling and there was no cover on the concrete floors apart from wooden pallets that the prisoners had gathered for themselves in order to sleep. The toilet facilities were totally inadequate, with people having to attend to their daily needs in buckets. There was a fence around the camp, but for the most part the inmates were kept in a shed under armed guard. There was one meal a day served in unsanitary conditions. The food was often rotten or if it was soup it was so watered down that it practically had no nutritional value. When inmates had to go for their meals, they were often forced to run through a cordon of guards who would beat them so fiercely that often the victims would forego their meals so as to avoid the further beating, thus further reducing their physical condition. Many of the inmates lost as much as half of their body weight during the months that they were kept in the camps. Some just died of malnutrition or as a consequence of their beating coupled with the malnutrition. The camp at its peak had a population of 1,500 inmates that were processed through the camp on a continual basis. The camp was made up almost exclusively of male inmates. It is anticipated that a great many of the prisoners that were taken to this camp have lost their lives. As I said, the camp at Omarska was on the fringe of a small town that bore the same name. The camp was at the site of an iron ore mine that had also ceased to function at this time. The camp was at the headquarters of the mine. It consisted of three main buildings which the witnesses refer to in the course of their evidence as the "white house", the "Administration building", the "garage or dumper" building. There is also a "small garage" but it is attached to the Administration building itself. In the centre of these buildings was a large concrete slab about 17 metres by 30 metres in size which was referred to by the prisoners as the "Pista". Many of the prisoners spent most of their time in this camp on this concrete open slab. Conditions at this camp in terms of food, hygiene and accommodation were much the same as at Keraterm, as was the treatment of the prisoners that were kept there. The camp was used to imprison mostly men, but again some women were kept there as well. The camp also had a special accommodation and special treatment meted out for leaders of the Muslim community, including professionals, such as doctors, lawyers and police officers. At its peak, the population of this camp had as many as 2,000 to 3,000 inmates, again who were processed through the camp on a continuous basis. It is estimated that a great many of the prisoners at this camp also lost their lives. Trnopolje is often regarded as the least brutal of the three camps, but conditions at this camp were very bad as well. The camp was made up of mixed sexes and children. The camp was located in the village of Trnopolje, approximately three kilometres from Kozarac. It changed its role from torture centre to detention centre on a number of occasions throughout 1992, and this mostly depended upon whether the International Committee of the Red Cross were about to visit or not. Sometimes it was fenced, but at other times the fences were removed. Many of the inmates could leave the camp with permission in order to get food and other supplies, but this freedom of movement depended upon the circumstances at the time. In Trnopolje camp, the inmates often made their own shelter out of plastic sheeting. Although conditions at this camp in terms of beating and brutality were for many of the prisoners better than Omarska and Keraterm, beatings, rapes, murders and other forms of abuse were, nevertheless, meted out in significant proportions. This camp was at the site of a school and the main prisoner accommodation was in a large gymnasium. The accommodation for the guards was in a building across the road from the camp, which the witnesses will also refer to as a "white house". This "white house" is not to be confused with the "white house" at Omarska. All the camps had their own command structure and the guards were specifically organised in shifts under shift bosses. There was co-ordination between the camps, which were run by the civilian authorities with military co-operation, particularly with the brutal interrogations. While some guards beat and killed prisoners from time to time, particular local Serbs would enter the camp and beat or kill Muslim inmates as they themselves had selected. The basis upon which these particular Bosnian Serbs were chosen to have special rights, including the rights of entry, is uncertain, but what appears is that the non-camp staff were allowed into the camps in order to commit particularly brutal acts of terror, presumably, in furtherance of the policy of ethnic cleansing. It would seem, however, that there is a category which these Serb torturers appeared to fit; they either had anti-Muslim, ethno-centric political dispositions which was conducive to the performance of these deeds or, alternatively, they were sadistically predisposed towards violence and took pleasure in inflicting tremendous pain and suffering upon the helpless victims, and thus served as a useful agent of the authorities. Tadic, the accused, was not a camp guard. He was a reserve policeman, but he was often seen entering the camps in the Prijedor region with lists of the names of Muslims who had been singled out for especially brutal treatment. When Tadic did enter the camps, he did so beyond the ordinary duties required of him as a policeman. Presumably, his reward for services rendered were special privileges, such as housing rights and the like. Later, he was to receive special status in the local administration and of being in charge of the distribution of humanitarian aid, a position of some importance and trust during these periods of shortages. Tadic seemed to be in a superior position to the camp guards and possibly even the camp commanders, but that was not as a consequence of any particular rank that he held in the Police Force but, it would seem, as a consequence of his political authority. The evidence will show that he was permitted to enter camps almost at random and to carry out assaults, murders, rapes and sexual assaults on the prisoners that he had selected. It seems that he was also permitted to bring his accomplices with him in order to assist him with his rampage of violence and terror. He, along with many others who performed these tasks, were seen with lists of names in their hands, which lists they consulted before calling out their victims especially selected for torture. Reference to these lists will be made by the witnesses on numerous occasions throughout the course of their evidence. In the mid-afternoon on a day in June 1992, the accused Tadic entered the Omarska camp with a group of Bosnian Serbs. They went to the large garage building known as the "hangar". They proceeded to call out the names of a number of people, including Emir Karabasic, Jasmin Hrnic, Enver Alic, Fikret Harambasic and Emir Beganovic. These and the other people called out were in a number of different rooms in the building. These men were then subjected to the most horrific beating and torture. Two other male prisoners were then called out forced to perform oral sex on Fikret Harambasic and then to sexually mutilate him. Karabasic, Hrnic, Alic and Harambasic died as a result of these assaults. Tadic again entered the Omarska camp on or about 10th July 1992. This time he went to the "white house" which was considered by all of the prisoners as the most dangerous place in the camp. Tadic was with a group of visiting Serbs. Prisoners from the white house and elsewhere were tortured outside the white house. When the Serbs were finished, Tadic threw a battered and dying Sefik Sivac, a restaurant owner from Kozarac and a former Muslim friend of Tadic, into a room in the white house. Sivac died from the beatings. Later, in July 1992, this time behind "the white house building" in the Omarska camp, Tadic in company of other Serbs from outside the camp severely beat and kicked Hakija Elezovic, Salih Elezovic, Sejad Sivac and other prisoners. The guards were wearing camouflage uniforms. They were using baseball bats and rubber sticks. One of them was using a spanner as a weapon. 10 or more were doing these beatings. The man who appeared to be in charge was Tadic. Tadic did not use any weapons, only his feet in the Karate fashion. Salih Elezovic and Sejad Sivac and other prisoners were found dead in the same spot later that day. Towards the end of June, or the first part of July, 1992, also near the "white house", Tadic and a group of Serbs from outside the camp ordered a group of prisoners to drink water like animals from puddles on the ground. They then jumped on their backs and beat them until they were unable to move. The victims were then removed from the area in a wheelbarrow. Tadic followed behind them and then forced the nozzle of a fire extinguisher into the mouth of one of the victims. On or about 8th July 1992, also in the white house, Tadic and a group of Serbs from outside the camp called out prisoners individually from one room in the "white house" to another room where they were beaten. One of the prisoners was Hase Icic. Hase Icic was taken to the torture room where Tadic, assisted by his accomplices, beat and kicked him until he was unconscious. Not all Muslims, Croats and disaffected Serbs were gathered up in the first round of ethnic cleansing after the Serb attack on Kozarac and the surrounding areas of the Opstina Prijedor; some people, especially old men, women and children, mostly Muslims, were permitted to stay in their villages. They were under a curfew and were not allowed to travel and as such were prisoners of the Serbs, albeit they did not have to reside in the camps. This situation of virtual house-arrest was not to last for long, because about 10 days after the initial sweep, these remnants of Muslims had to confront their turn to be ethnically cleansed. In the villages of Jaskici and Sivic, located southeast of Prijedor town, on or about 14th June 1992, Tadic with a group of armed Serbs came to the village in order to further the Serbian cause of ethnic cleansing. Tadic and the other Serbs entered Jaskici, jumping fencing like hunters chasing game. They yelled for all the people in the houses to come out. Those inhabitants who were outside or who came out were made to lie on the road. Abaz Jaskic, born in 1942, and his son, Nijis Jaskic, born in 1964, were killed in the village that day. The Serbs went to the home of Sakib and Osme Elkasevic. They along with Alija Javor, who was not a resident of the village, were also killed that day. Salko Jaskic, Beido Balic and Sefik Balic were ordered out of Salko's house by the Serbs and told to lie down on the road. Ismet Jaskic, Meho Kenjar, Adam Jakupovic and Nijas Elkasevic and Ilijas Elkasevic were also driven down the road and ordered to lie down in front of the house of Salko Jaskic. While they were on the ground, the men were all beaten by both the Serb groups who were using fence posts and other such weapons. All of the Serbs, including the accused Tadic, appeared to be participating. Some of the Serbs were walking on the back of the old man, Meho Kenjar, as if to crush him. None of these Muslim men were armed, nor did they offer any resistance. Those that were not killed were taken away from this place and have not been seen since. Throughout the most part of 1992, the Serb authorities pursued a campaign of persecution of the non-Serbs of the Prijedor Opstina. They persecuted the non-Serbs because they wanted the Opstina completely free of Muslim or Croatian influence. Tadic participated with the Serb forces in this persecution which manifested itself in the attack, destruction and plunder of Bosnian Muslims and Croat residential areas, the seizure and imprisonment of thousands of Muslims and Croats under brutal conditions in the camps at Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje, and the deportation and/or expulsion of the majority of the Muslim and Croat residents of the Opstina by force or threat of force. During this time, Serb forces, including Dusko Tadic, subjected Muslims and Croats inside and outside the camps to a campaign of terror and psychological abuse. Tadic was actively involved, as I said earlier, in the attack on Kozarac. His participation in the firing of the flares to illuminate the village at night for the artillery and tank guns as the village was being shelled and physically assisting in the seizure, collection, segregation and forced transfer to detention camps of the majority of the non-Serb population of the area is also evidence of his participation. Tadic also took part in the killing and beating of a number of seized persons, including the killing of an old man and a woman near the cemetery in "old" Kozarac, the beatings of at least two former policemen from Kozarac at a road junction in the village of Kozarac and the beating of a number of Muslim males who had been seized and detained at the Prijedor military barracks. The fact that Tadic physically took part in the killing, torture, sexual assault and other beatings of many of the detainees at Omarska camp and participated in the beating of detainees and looting at the Keraterm camp is further evidence of his participation in this campaign of persecution. In addition to the above, and during the period 25th May 1992 to 31st December 1992, Tadic physically participated and otherwise assisted in the transfer to and the unlawful confinement in Trnopolje camp of non-Serbs in the Kozarac area. During the period September 1992 to December 1992, in Trnopolje camp and in the adjacent areas, Tadic physically took part or otherwise participated in the killing of more than 30 detainees, including a group of mail detainees executed in a plum orchard adjacent to the camp. Tadic also physically took part or otherwise participated in the torture of more than 12 female detainees, including several gang rapes, which occurred in the camp and at a "white house" adjacent to the camp. Concurrent with the attack and seizure of the non-Serb populations in Kozarac and surrounding area, the Serb forces plundered and destroyed the homes, businesses and properties of non-Serbs. The seizure, transfer and detention of the non-Serb populations and the plundering and destruction of their property continued throughout this campaign of persecution of the non-Serb population. Tadic was aware of the widespread nature of the plunder and destruction of personal and real property of the non-Serbs and was physically involved in this plunder and destruction himself. The subjugation and persecution of prisoners at the camps was achieved in similar ways. New prisoners were usually greeted with beatings upon their arrival. This happened while the camp commander often looked on. On other occasions prisoners were not fed for several days after their arrival at the camp, and even after that they only received the most meagre of daily rations. At the height of summer, water was often withheld and, if served, it was often contaminated. Toilet facilities and hygiene conditions were inhuman. As if all this treatment were not enough, the prisoners were then forced to sing or to listen to Serbian nationalist songs. Almost all the prisoners were subjected to interrogation, which often meant beatings at the same time. Beatings were rampant, especially at night and at meal times. Prisoners were killed almost every night, with their corpses being stacked up awaiting removal by trucks in the morning. Most of the camp guards were from the villages near the camps. However, the interrogation was often conducted by the local police and school teachers. From time to time members of the special military forces and some local civilians came to the camps and administered particularly brutal beatings and other measures of torture. In early August 1992, the international press and the International Committee of the Red Cross were granted permission to visit these camps. Immediately before the visits, most of the prisoners from Omarska and Keraterm were transferred to Trnopolje and Manjaca. A large number were put to death in one last attempt to wipe out the Muslim population. Those prisoners who survived the ordeal, and in most cases only did so because the camps were exposed by the international media and the International Committee of the Red Cross, were eventually allowed to leave the camps provided they relinquished their property and left the region. By this time, the Muslim leaders and intellectuals had mostly been wiped out, their homes and mosques destroyed. The ones who had survived had no jobs and what was once their home was now a hostile, unprotected and foreign environment. A whole ethnic community had, effectively, been destroyed in that area. Ethnic cleansing had been achieved. In February 1994, Tadic was arrested in Munich, Germany, by the German Police as a result of their investigation into the activities of the accused. On 11th October 1994, in Munich, the accused was questioned by the German Police in the Munich Standelheim prison. Tadic was informed that he could either speak about the accusations made against him or he could remain silent, and that he was entitled to the assistance of a defence counsel of his own choosing. Defence counsel was subsequently appointed for Tadic and his lawyer attended the Police Station where he was interviewed by the Police. The accused informed the German Police that in 1991 he was appointed Chairman of the Election Committee in the Kozarac area or, more particularly, one electoral district in the Kozarac area. Tadic said that individuals who were appointed to their respective voting districts were determined by the municipality of Prijedor upon the proposal of existing parties. He said: "I was chairman along with three other Serbs who had been appointed who were responsible for how the voting went on there in organisational terms". Tadic said that in May 1992 he was appointed a member of the local Civic Forum, the role of which was to attempt to resolve the tensions that had developed between the various parties in the Kozarac and Prijedor regions. Tadic said that the Forum was composed of eight Muslims and three Serbs. He also said that, as far as he could remember, the war began in Kozarac on 24th May 1992. He also said that he was never involved in the war and he had moved out of Kozarac on 23rd May in 1992 and lived with his family in Banja Luka. The accused said that he lived with his family in Banja Luka until 6th or 18th July 1992, when he was mobilized to Prijedor as a reserve traffic policeman where upon he was subsequently assigned to the village of Orlovci. Tadic said that in October 1992 he was active on a temporary basis in Kozarac as Secretary of the local authority, and on 21st December 1992 he was officially appointed to that office. He said that the local SDS Committee was founded in October 1992, and that he had acted only as a temporary Chairman until he was formally appointed in December 1992. He said that at the end of 1992 he was appointed as an intermediary or contact with the International Committee of the Red Cross. In March 1993, he was appointed by the President of the Municipal Assembly to arrange the "civilian life" in the Kozarac area. He goes on to say that Kozarac at that time was practically dead, "... the village had to be rebuilt". During this time he had an exemption from police and military service. He said that in August 1993, after encountering some difficulties in the Prijedor region, he sent his wife and children to Germany and he fled to Banja Luka from where he subsequently went to Belgrade after unsuccessfully obtaining refugee status. He said he came to Germany as a member of a Karate team to attend a tournament in December 1993 where he was granted a short-term residence visa. Tadic denied that he had done anything to harm the Muslims or that he was ever in the Omarska camp. "I have never set foot in that place". He said that he was in Trnopolje camp five times, but this was an open camp and people could move about freely, and that he also attended this camp on humanitarian missions. Tadic admitted that in the Police he was provided with an automatic rifle, a police baton, a cross-chest belt which contained bullets and an undefined supply of ammunition, and that he personally owned a pistol which he wore on duty sometimes, especially at night-time, and he carried a knife with a 15 centimetre blade which he used primarily at meal times, and all of this was worn while he was on duty as a traffic policeman. The record of the interview between the German authorities and Tadic was recorded in writing, was read to him in his own tongue and was approved and signed by both Tadic and his counsel. Is that a convenient time, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. If your Honours please, on 8th November 1994 the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia presented to Chamber One of the Tribunal a request that the Tadic investigation, then being conducted by the Federal Republic of Germany, be deferred to the Tribunal pursuant to Rules 9 and 10 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The request was granted by the Chamber. The Prosecutor presented an indictment against the accused for confirmation on 8th February. The indictment was subsequently confirmed by His Honour Judge Karibi-Whyte on 13th February 1995, and a formal request for transfer to The Hague was sent to the German authorities. The accused was transferred to The Hague on 24th April 1995 and attended his initial appearance. If your Honours please, the Prosecution will prove that the accused, Dusko Tadic, also called Dule by friends and members of his family, was born on 1st October 1955 in the village of Kozarac. His father's name was Ostoje born in 1920 in the village of Babici. He died in 1990. His mother’s name is Staka born in 1920 in the village of Veljko. She is currently living in Kozarac. He has three brothers: Mladen, Stojan and Ljubomir and no sisters. He was married in 1979 and has two daughters. His family was well known in the area, as his father, two uncles and grandfather fought in World War II and his grandmother had been incarcerated in camps during World War II. Tadic commenced schooling at about the age of 7 and attended primary school in Kozarac. He then attended secondary school in Belgrade. At the completion of his schooling in 1976 and 1977 he carried out compulsory service in the JNA for a period of 14 months. In 1980 and 1984 he worked in Banja Luka as a construction worker and in 1984 he went to Libya with the intention of obtaining employment. He returned in 1985. On his return to Bosnia he worked in the town of Sisak in Croatia in a private company installing carpentry works. He remained in this employment until 1989 when he returned to Kozarac and commenced to build a cafe bar which was to be called Nipon. In December 1990 he opened a cafe bar and ran it until the commencement of the war in 1992. In Kozarac the accused lived in Marsala Tita Street 36 in the area of Kozarac known as the central commune. The Prosecution will establish that in the latter part of 1990, possibly August, the accused first joined the Serbian Democratic Party known as the SDS. The Prosecution expects to call in excess of 80 witnesses. The evidence will be made up of segments of proof according to the requirements of the charges. The special requirement associated with international crimes will be dealt with in the evidence first. The evidence will consist of a mixture of expert and special fact witnesses. For example, the expert witnesses will opine on the question of the international nature of the armed conflict, the widespread or systematic nature of the crimes and the political and historical background of the conflict. They will also give relevant evidence going to the status of the victims vis-a-vis their aggressors. The special fact witnesses will give evidence relevant to the showing that the armed forces of the Serbs operating in Bosnia contained an international element, namely, participation in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. They will also give evidence of the widespread or systematic nature of the attack. In other words, this evidence will show that the attack was not some isolated affair in Opstina Prijedor, but it was a much wider, co-ordinated and well-executed a strategy across the whole of Bosnia. The expert witnesses will give evidence of the political makeup of the communities which is of special significance in understanding the nature of the persecution of the non-Serb community. The evidence of the special fact witnesses who will be called following the evidence of Dr. Gow, of necessity will be detailed because they will relate in a summary fashion the events which occurred to them in another place, in another Opstina, but at about the same time. Their evidence in scope is almost as wide as the evidence in scope as is called in this case. Then the witnesses will be called who will attest to the particular charges in the indictment. These witnesses will present their evidence, as much as it is possible, according to the chronological date order of events; starting with the events of Kozarac in the early part of the war, followed by the evidence of what happened to people taken to the Prijedor barracks or to the camps. Then there will follow evidence of what occurred at Omarska Camp, at the villages of Jaskici and Sivci, then Keraterm Camp and then, finally, Trnopolje Camp. The Prosecution case will conclude with a number of investigation witnesses and medical and forensic expert witnesses. It is the Prosecution case that all the evidence will be relevant to the charge of persecution. For some of the witnesses the recounting of what occurred to them may cause them stress, more so than what one may ordinarily encounter in a national forum. The recounting by a number of people of the same events will reflect the horror and confusion of the occasion. This may sometimes prevent the neat and orderly dovetailing of the evidence, but such minor variations or descriptions will only serve to reinforce the reliability and integrity of their evidence, because it is almost beyond human capacity for two human beings to witness such appalling scenes and to later recount them with identical descriptions of what occurred. There is also the issue of multiple languages and the imprecision of the interpretation process. As has already been observed in the pretrial stage, a great deal of accuracy is bound to be lost in the translation process. There is no statement taken during the course of the investigation that will be a verbatim report of what the witnesses say. The Prosecution case rests primarily on eyewitness testimony. However, the case is not totally devoid of exhibits. For example, the expert witness Dr. Gow and Greve in particular will refer to a number of documents in support of their testimony. In addition to documents, there will also be some video evidence referred to by these and other witnesses. There will be a number of maps produced to explain where and when things occurred. Dr. Gow, in particular, will give his evidence almost entirely through documents which will be displayed on the television monitor, which exhibits will be tendered by reference to what one sees on the monitor. An index of these documents has been prepared and will be distributed to your Honours, to the Defence, the Registrar as an aide memoir, so that helpfully we can follow the complex numbering system which has been brought about by the intrusion of the computer technology into the process. There will also be a considerable number of photographs introduced into the evidence. These photographs were taken by the Tribunal investigators when they first visited Opstina Prijedor in January of this year. We also expect that some of the witnesses may wish to sketch plans or diagrams to assist them in the giving of their evidence. If your Honour pleases, as most of the legal issues, including the elements of the offence, have now been addressed in the Prosecutor's pretrial brief and the Defence's responses thereto, it is not my intention to recanvass these issues in my opening. However, I expect that there will be much discussion on these legal issues at a later stage in the proceedings. Unless I can assist your Honours further, that is my opening.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Will the Defence wish to present an opening statement at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we prefer to deliver the opening statement in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Today.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am in a position to call evidence, your Honour, but I do not know whether that would be convenient, if Mr. Wladimiroff would perhaps like to follow immediately after me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will proceed until 1 o'clock. So the question now becomes what do we with this hour that we have? I gather you want to present your opening statements so there will be continuity. How much time do you expect you will need, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, Rule 84 of our few Rules provides that before presentation of evidence by the Prosecutor each party may make an opening statement. The Defence may, however, elect to make its statement after the Prosecutor has concluded his presentation of the evidence and before the presentation of evidence for the Defence. The rule really does not envision that the Prosecutor would present a portion of its evidence and then the Defence begin its opening statement. You of course may elect to wait to give your opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I was under the impression that the Prosecution had concluded its presentation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Its opening statement, yes. It is now your turn to present your opening statement or, if you wish, you may wait until the Prosecution concludes the offering of its evidence. Now I understand your position, you would rather begin your opening statement and just go right through without an interruption. We have interpreters present here and their job, I think, is more difficult than anyone's job in the courtroom. I do not know, we might share in some of the difficulties. So we really could not continue to hear your opening statement in its entirety. So what we suggest is that you begin your opening statement now, if that is how you wish to proceed, or you may wait until you wish to present your evidence on your case, as you wish. Then we will recess at 1 o'clock as we normally do. We can certainly keep your opening statement in context. We will not forget anything that has been said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I appreciate that, your Honour. Maybe we could compromise on starting at an earlier time this afternoon, because I rather prefer to do it in one presentation and not be interrupted by lunch.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not have a problem with it, but, as I say, we have other persons who expect a recess at a certain time because of the conditions under which they operate. Let me see what can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If we start at an earlier time then I think we will not lose too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think it is worked out. We are very flexible, but in this age of technology and everything else we have to get permission from other persons. We have a solution. We will stand in recess then now for an hour and a half rather than taking our lunch break at 1, and so we will return at a few minutes after 1.30 and you will then begin your opening statements, Mr. Wladimiroff. Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Your Honours, in the 17th century, the famous Dutch author on international law, Hugo Grotius, wrote that where justice fails, war begins, in Latin: "Ubi iuditia deficiunt, incipit bellum". Indeed, history has shown that in times of conflict the civilised language of war and justice has been shouted down all over the world by thunder of arms and violence over and over again. People, leaders and states have so far not been able to administer basic rules of humanitarian law under all circumstances. Efforts of the international community to recognise violations of humanitarian law, to create legal instruments to prevent further violations and to establish bodies to prosecute such violations did, however, not bring these violations to an end. Despite the atrocities of the Second World War, people all over the world have suffered from a lack of respect for humanitarian law and even today countless people still suffer. The establishment of the International Tribunal for the Prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia is intended to be an answer to the appeal of all those victims, named and unnamed, who suffered and still suffer from the terrible consequences of the violent breaking up of the former Yugoslavia. The establishment of the Tribunal, however, could not end the misery of the common man. It was the Dayton Agreement that silenced the weapons, perhaps creating a platform for peace. The importance of the Tribunal, though, is that it may bring justice, if it will not only show that it will investigate and prosecute all major violations without any prejudice to any party to the conflict, but if it will also conduct uncompromised fair trials. A failure to meet both an undisputable impartiality to the conflict and the highest standard of fairness of trial will only fuel new hate, and further retaliation. You may wonder, your Honours, what this all has to do with the case of Dusko Tadic, the individual who stands trial today. The strength of the Defence in the Tadic case will be severely affected by the weakness of the Tribunal itself.
