Therefore, the Defence has to start by considering the inherent shortcomings of the Tribunal and only then will be able to present its case in its proper context. The grave and onerous task of bringing to justice those who are suspected of committing the most heinous crimes in the course of a long and bloody conflict will arouse great emotions from all sides during the trial. But the professional participants in this court, listening to the witnesses, must master the ability to separate truth from lies and human error. The Tribunal has not been established to satisfy the victims only, but to bring justice to all, including the accused. The Tribunal must be wary of the desires for revenge and a need for a scapegoat. Bringing justice to all in this first case on trial before the Tribunal requires that it should not respond to the perfect pressure. It should disregard the public cry for a sentence of the first accused to stand trial. On the contrary, it should without dispute conduct a fair trial, whatever the outcome of this case may be. Justice will only be satisfied with a conviction if there is certainty beyond any reasonable doubt that the man who you see sitting in the dock here is the same man who committed the crimes of which you will hear in the weeks to come. If, as we maintain, it cannot be sufficiently proved, and Dusko Tadic is innocent of these offences, then the temptation to use the lack of clarity in the law to satisfy an international community hunger for a verdict of guilty must be resisted at all costs. The thirst for revenge must not be satisfied at the well of polluted justice. I would respectfully urgently enjoin you to keep in mind at all times the importance of reaching the right verdict on the evidence before you on the basis of a fair understanding of the law. In this respect, we must keep in mind that this is the first case which the Tribunal has to try. As an experiment, it should not be conducted at the expense of the defendant. Where the law of the Tribunal is not clear on vital issues, these issues should unquestionably be dealt with in favour of the defendant; because in a fair administration of justice there is no room for experiments with a defendant as a guinea-pig. It is the responsibility of the Tribunal to protect a defendant against vague laws and vague procedures. If the law is not clear, the defendant should be given the benefit of protection; protection against prosecution on the basis of novelties yet to be sorted out; protection against an unprecedented extension of a reasonable understanding of the law. In avoiding and redressing unfair interpretations of new law, you have the full support of the Defence. If this Tribunal is not at all times vigilant to avoid the risk of speculative and, therefore, wrongful convictions, it will be responsible for causing further wrongful and unnecessary suffering. The Defence is confident that the Court shares the same concerns and will serve the cause of justice at all costs. Your Honours, the trial of our client started in unfavourable circumstances. The prosecution of Dusko Tadic started while the war in Bosnia Herzegovina was still going on. It was only in January of this year that it was possible to enter the area for a proper investigation of the case. As long as the fighting was going on, large parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not be reached. Both parties, the Prosecution as well as the Defence, have been affected by these limitations; and the risk has arisen that the trial will be conducted before all the facts are known. This is even more serious as one of the parties is affected more heavily by this limitation than the other. All the Prosecution witnesses live now outside the area. All the Defence witnesses live within the area. The Prosecution may have had its problems, but the Defence has been seriously handicapped in the preparation of its case. The Defence is particularly handicapped in the investigation of the facts. Inherent to the first case before the Tribunal is the fact that there is uncertainty how to apply the law. Here two issues arise: As for the crimes, the Tribunal does not provide either party with a complete certainty. The trial starts today, while only last Friday the Judges told our client ,"We do not know which elements are necessary to prove the offences charged"; neither can the Tribunal provide the parties with clear procedural law. Rules have been developed that have not been tested previously and which are incomplete. It is also unique that both the suitability and the contents of the Rules have not been determined by a legislator but by the Judges themselves. The Tribunal cannot give any guarantees as to whether its Rules will be applied in the area of the war or elsewhere. Parties have to wait to see whether persons or authorities in the area or elsewhere will co-operate with the Tribunal. Up to now this does not seem to have always been the case. The Statute and the Rules do not offer any structure within which the parties can achieve their aims for case preparation through states and individuals who have been involved in the war. For example, unlike National Courts, the Tribunal has no police force of its own to bring witnesses to the hearing. In this respect, the Defence is affected more heavily by the absence of such powers. Experience up to now has shown that the Prosecution, due to its official status as an organ of the Tribunal, has been able to obtain co-operation from national authorities. Countries other than those which used to make up Yugoslavia are, so it is said, co-operating well with the Prosecution. The same cannot be said for the Defence. The consequence of all these unfortunate circumstances is that the trial against our client begins in an incomplete setting. This is not without significance for the further course of this trial, and the final question which has to be asked is whether a fair trial is possible at all. A further problem is the lack of clearly defined criteria for the prosecution of the accused. Bearing in mind the fact that not everyone who might be suspected would actually be prosecuted, it is unfortunate that the Prosecution has not been clear as to what criteria it is applying. Thus, it appears that the prosecution of those accused is not based upon established guidelines, but on arbitrary consideration such as the availability of data and suspects. This gives rise to the question of whether Dusko Tadic would ever have been prosecuted had not the Germans come across him by accident in Munich; we shall probably never know. It is clear, however, that the lack of defined and public criteria has blown the case against Dusko Tadic out of all proportion. Already the danger seems evident that the case is viewed as a symbol of everything that happened in the area, and that Dusko Tadic has been portrayed as the prototype of a war criminal. It requires little argument to show that this has a disproportionate effect on the evidence in the case and it may influence the judgment of that evidence. If the first persons suspected of being involved in war crimes are tried and only later those responsible for causing the conflict in the first place (and here I hold the politicians in all the parties in the former Yugoslavia responsible), then there is the danger that the judgment in this first case will be unbalanced. Individual responsibility does not stand by itself, but should also be judged against the background of the climate created by the political elite. The Tribunal's task is, therefore, far from easy. There are many circumstances that make it difficult to perform your task. With limited legal instruments, limited possibilities for enforcement and incomplete data, there is the danger of high media exposure and low quality justice. Where should then the limits be drawn? It has rightly been said that without a proper defence a fair trial is impossible. Under normal circumstances, it is not difficult to approve the working of the machinery of justice as it applies to both the Prosecution and the Defence. This case, this trial, though, is not normal. The circumstances under which the trial takes place are especially bad. I have just shown which circumstances may prevent the Tribunal from fulfilling its task properly. The question, to what extent the presence of the Defence justifies the assumption that there is a fair trial, has been an issue from the very beginning. The real issue here is whether we are able to conduct a proper defence. For the Defence, the ultimate question is whether, under all these circumstances I have put to you, a fair trial is possible at all. The fact that this trial is starting today does not provide us with a definite answer. It should be seriously considered that the conditions required for a fair trial may ultimately not be fulfilled. The reasons have already been given. Uncertainty as to whether at a certain stage a point is reached at which the conclusion has to be that a fair trial is no longer possible is a great, great cause for concern to the Defence. An important consideration for the Defence has been whether the trial should be postponed. Since November last year, the Defence has asked for a postponement since we were not ready for the trial. But it should be remembered that our client has been in detention on remand for over two years now, including the German time. In our opinion, a further postponement of the trial in the hope of better days is no longer justified. Again, where are the limits? What conditions should be fulfilled? What conditions should be fulfilled now? In the Defence's opinion, these limits have been crossed if we are unable to call the witnesses necessary for the presentation of our case to testify. On this point, no arguments on the quality of the trial should be considered, even though the Prosecution might say that a fair trial does not mean a perfect trial. There is no scale with "a fair trial" at the bottom and "a perfect trial" at the top. In the Defence's opinion, there is only one standard here. The only possible trial is a fair trial and a fair trial is the only possible trial. Thus, the question is not whether a few witnesses can or cannot testify; every witness called by the Defence will be called after a careful consideration as to how the Defence should be conducted. We have carefully selected our alibi witnesses. We have notified so far 36 witnesses. The Prosecution has notified us of between 88 to 120 witnesses. We hope it has been as careful. Every witness selected by the Defence is of, indeed, great importance. The question is not whether one of them can or cannot come. Even if the Tribunal is prepared to create the circumstances (as it now has done to some extent) under which it will be possible to hear the witnesses called by the Defence, there is the further issue as to whether they will give, in fact, evidence and that is still to see. At least after this morning's rulings some relief has now been provided, but the further problem of subjective fear of the witnesses has not been resolved yet. The people living in this area are scattered, they are threatened, they are afraid and the local authorities are answerable for that. Under such conditions it is very hard to conduct a fair trial. Should it appear that legal and factual circumstances prevent the Tribunal from finding the truth, then, in our opinion, the limit of fairness is exceeded. The intention to conduct a fair trial is not sufficient; the point is that all conditions for a fair trial should actually be fulfilled. Your Honours, as is clear from previous remarks, the uncertainty as to the law poses a great problem. If we take into consideration the indictment, then two questions will play a role during the process: Firstly, the vagueness of the indicted offences and, secondly, the manner in which they are described in the indictment. In all civilised systems of criminal law, we find the principle of legitimacy. There can be no offence without a precise previous legal provision. In this case this requirement of criminal law is at best insufficiently met. The core of the problem is that this case, unfortunately, does not involve offences clearly defined beforehand, but offences assumed to be punishable without the exact content being determined. What is punishable is thus not based on a legislative provision but on customary law. Your Honours, law covered by custom and subject to change may be acceptable for the international relations between states. It cannot be acceptable when applied to an individual charged with criminal offences. This problem is not only a cause of concern to the Defence, but also to the Prosecution. They have made it clear, they too are uncertain what exactly they will have to prove. The Defence is of the opinion that in this case the contents of a criminal provision are not predetermined. The Prosecution should not decide to prosecute such undefined offences and thereby expose an accused to the risk of speculative prosecution. In the opinion of the Defence, this is not a usual discussion on the interpretation of a certain criminal provision. This, your Honours, is about the fundamental questions of what elements constitute criminal offences. Here as well the special circumstances under which this Tribunal is operating play a role. Due to the mix of common and civil law, the problem of legality has a different consequence than in either one of these systems. Since the Tribunal relies mainly on the common law's accusatory system, the absence of a jury causes a systemic failure. If there were a jury, the judge would, after the defence has been put forward, inform them as to the law applicable and give a decisive answer what elements constitute the criminal offence, for only then can the jury be capable of reaching a verdict. In the jury system, the fact that the judge determines what law is applicable after the evidence has been put forward does not pose a problem since the question of guilt is only resolved by the jury afterwards. In this case, however, the Judges are also the jury; your Honours will determine whether the accused is guilty or not. This at least gives rise to the theoretical question at which moment you, so to speak, instruct yourselves; and whether parties will know this assumed instruction, so that it will become clear to us what criteria you are using to determine the question of guilt. Also here we have two issues. If we are to assume that the criteria applied by the Trial Chamber are only to become clear in the verdict, then there is a danger that in putting forward the evidence the Defence cannot anticipate what your Honours might consider relevant to determine Dusko Tadic's guilt. Consistency in the proceedings becomes a severe problem, and the accused is exposed to the risk of a speculative trial. Moreover, the Defence believes that this situation should be prevented to avoid diminishing trust in the Tribunal. It would be very sad if people were to think or, even worse, if the accused thought that the Judges are working the other way around, first determining guilt and then explaining the law. The problems relating to the principle of legality do not stand alone, I am afraid. Matters are made worse by the way in which the indictment has been drafted. The Defence has made it known on previous occasions that it considers the time frame of the indictment too broad. The Defence wishes to point out that we are concerned that in the weeks, and maybe even months, to come evidence or witnesses will not clarify this. The Defence fears that the optimism of the Prosecution that everything shall become clear when their case is presented is not justified. Should this not be the case, then this would lay a disproportionate burden on the Defence in establishing the alibi of the defendant. The Defence would also like to point out that this indictment puts the accused in a position of double jeopardy, a well known principle in criminal justice systems, by alleging the general offence of prosecution in count 1 and relying on the same allegations in counts 2 to 4 or, should I say now it has been withdraw, 5 to 34. Finally, the Defence has a great fear of prejudice caused by the number of allegations. The Defence is concerned that separate evidence on one count may be wrongly considered as evidence on another. This mixture of allegations may be, if we do not take care, a recipe for a miscarriage of justice. Your Honours, I have already mention the problems regarding accessibility and availability of evidence. The consequence of this is that the Defence realises that this trial will probably not provide an example of a successful search for the truth, but a very limited attempt to do so. The trial system developed by the Tribunal is based to a large extent on an accusatory system in which both parties have the opportunity to present their case. This system presumes that each party is able to present its case, and each party is able to do so to the same extent. As long as the question of availability of witnesses has not been solved to everyone's satisfaction, the Rules regarding presentation of evidence seems arbitrary. At this stage, we should distinguish between the pretrial proceedings and the proceedings before the Trial Chamber. In the pretrial proceedings, the Defence has had to build its case from that initial appearance onwards; whereas the Prosecution had already built up a case before issuing the indictment. This head start is a normal problem under normal circumstances, and I would not have mentioned it in my opening speech had it not been for the problems which have presented themselves within their proceedings. The Rules provide specific provisions to enable the parties to ascertain the relevant facts. These are legal instruments available other than the powers given to the Prosecution to force states to co-operate in the pretrial investigation. The Defence has no power whatsoever to enlist anyone's co-operation in providing relevant facts. The Defence's activities preceding the trial depends solely upon the voluntary co-operation of others. The reality is that this Tribunal sits in North West Europe. Any orders made would have no effect in the Republika Srpska. The Dayton Agreement has had no effect on this situation. Article 29 of the Statute is a dead letter too, since the Republika Srpska was not officially recognised and the government in Sarajevo (who would formally be the addressee of Article 29) did not exert any authority in the Serbian parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Tribunal was aware of this at the pretrial stage. The Prosecution was aware of this at the pretrial stage. The Defence have had to bear the consequences at the pretrial stage. In other words, the Tribunal and the Prosecution knew that the Defence would be working in a procedural vacuum; that the Defence had to prepare a case without a single legal instrument to support it. Everything, therefore, that the Defence has been able to achieve so far is the result of our own negotiations with authorities and individuals and not of any provision of the Tribunal. The pretrial proceedings have shown a serious inequality of arms in that all the Prosecution's witnesses are outside the Srpske Republic, and that all authorities except those of the Srpske Republic have fully co-operated with the Prosecution in this case. In the weeks to come we shall see how this lack of equality of arms at the pretrial stage affects the trial itself. In addition, the Rules of evidence are so open that only case law can determine their precise content. In these circumstances, the Defence requests the Tribunal to apply principles of admissibility of evidence based upon reliability. Your Honours, the court will hear a great deal of evidence from witnesses for the Prosecution about events which happened in the long hot summer of 1992 in the Opstina of Prijedor. It is not disputed that terrible things happened during the conflict in the area, and particularly in the camp at Omarska. As a result of what happened, all the Prosecution witnesses you will hear from have left the area and are now living as refugees in other countries. It is not for those of us who have not experienced such things to say what effect they have on the heart and the minds of those who have. It is neither the right nor the intention of the Defence to be belittle the tremendous suffering about which you will hear. However, it is both our right and our duty to defend Dusko Tadic against the allegations made by these witnesses. I have two very general observations to make, the first is this: Ever since these camps were discovered by Western journalists in August 1992, the international interest in events in this area in general and in the camps, in particular, have been intense. There can be few who failed to see and be deeply affected by the pictures of emaciated figures looking out from behind a wire fence at Trnopolje. As a result of this interest, journalists have pursued many of those who will be giving evidence in this court in attempts to provide the world with news and stories for their readers and listeners. It is our case that many witnesses have adopted the accounts of fellow prisoners, having heard or read these in the media. Also, when inmates of these camps were released or moved on to other locations, they talked to each other about their experiences. You will hear in the coming weeks and months that one witness, in particular, has told his "story" concerning a notorious incident in Omarska to well over half of the other witnesses claiming to have seen those same events. We do not require the assistance of a psychologist to convince us of the importance and the power of suggestion. It is something you come across in every day life. If several people witness the same event, they do not all recall every detail, but when they discuss the events together afterwards, a composite story emerges. Rumour becomes truth. Rumour becomes truth. People convince themselves with ease that they have seen and heard things which they did not and could not have seen and heard. Their account is based on what others have told them. This also can be a recipe for unreliability for which a miscarriage of justice is made. If this can happen in the most ordinary circumstances, how much greater is the risk that it will happen in extraordinary ones? The situation of which you will hear in the course of the Prosecution case is quite outside the experience and understanding of any ordinary person. These witnesses had by their own account been forcibly evicted from their homes in the course of a bloody conflict, had been separated from their families and their friends, had seen many people who were close to them killed by their aggressors. They were kept in appallingly cramped conditions in the burning heat of a Bosnian summer with little food or water, fearful at every moment of torture and death. It was in these conditions that they witnessed the events of which they will come and tell you at this trial. Such circumstances, your Honours, are able to provide both the stuff of rumour and the need for a scapegoat. It is not the fact of their suffering which is questioned by the Defence, but the reliability of evidence obtained from people who, apparently, witnessed the events under these conditions. Many people were told, either at the time or afterwards, that Dusko Tadic had been committing crimes in the camps. How many of these people have fitted second-hand accounts into their own accounts, to fill gaps or identify a person who they did not, in fact, see at all? Your Honours, Dusko Tadic was a Serb, a Serb who lived in the centre of the Muslim community of Kozarac, the community which was so brutally expelled from its home during the summer of 1992. 18 months later, Dusko Tadic himself went to Germany where many of his former neighbours were now living. It is not difficult to imagine the reaction of those people who had been forced from their homes to a neighbour who was a Serb. They were Muslims, and the hatred which now existed against Serbs within the Muslim community was such that to be a Serb was to be associated with a people against whom they would go at lengths to take revenge. The prejudice that exists in this case cannot be underestimated. When Dusko Tadic went to Germany in 1993, he offered himself up as an easy victim to those who wanted revenge against the Serb people. It is inconceivable that he would have gone to live amongst the very people he is alleged to have persecuted, if their allegations were true. It is the task of this court to see through the distorting glass of prejudice to the truth which lies beyond. A witness who has suffered must be pitied for his suffering, but he should not be believed because of his suffering. It is nowhere argued that one who has suffered is for that reason more likely to tell the truth; indeed, the reverse may often be the case. This, your Honours, then is the Defence case, that the witnesses who you will hear giving evidence against the defendant are doing so, if not by inadmissible hearsay, as the result either of an honest but distorted and false belief, or of prejudice against the Serb people. Again, I say to you that Dusko Tadic stands charged as an individual, and the crimes of others cannot and should not be laid at his feet. Your Honours, in presenting the Defence case, we will not be presenting evidence relating to camps because it is not for the Defence to dispute what happened in the camps. The Defence case is simply that Dusko Tadic was not involved in the camps in any capacity. I will present evidence that Dusko Tadic had no access to the camps and that he was not in a privileged position suggested by the Prosecution this morning. In preparing the defence, we have struggled with the hostility and suspicion with which the Tribunal is viewed in the Serb Republic and, in particular, in the Prijedor area. Those in power in this area have blocked avenues of investigation, not only to the Prosecution, but also to the Defence. It might be thought that they would be eager to help Dusko Tadic in his defence at this trial and treat him as one of their own. This, your Honours, has not been the case. The Defence of Dusko Tadic has been prepared with little or no help from the Prijedor authorities, and there have been active attempts to prevent us from obtaining evidence on behalf of our client to prove his innocence. Witnesses in the area who held any police or military authority have been barred from talking to the Defence. False rumours have been promulgated about the desire of the Tribunal to arrest anyone who came forward to give evidence. Our activities have been closely monitored, and witnesses who are known to have been co-operating with us have suffered threats to themselves and their families. One high ranking official said, and I quote, "No one can order me to allow the witnesses for the Defence to be investigated in my area. No witness from my area can make a statement without my consent. I can be replaced from my post as head, but in that case I will cede the whole region to Croatia. We have over 4 million tonnes of iron ore in storage which we will send to Sisak to be processed and we'll get the money". After having been asked whether the people of Krajina would agree to the succession, he said: "Who is asking the people? Fuck the people!" May I repeat the quote which has emerged from the lips of the Prosecution in recent months: "A fair trial is not a perfect trial". Your Honours, we have become aware, indeed, of the impossibility of anything approaching a fair trial in such compromising circumstances. Our aim has been to ensure that at least a fair trial would not be impossible from the very beginning. Despite the difficulties we have encountered and continue to encounter, we have persisted and we have succeeded in building a strong and convincing Defence case. We believe it will be impossible for you to convict Dusko Tadic if we will be able to present the Defence case to its full extent. We have done this to satisfy our determination that Dusko Tadic will against all the odds have a fair trial which produces what we believe is the only possible verdict in this case, a verdict of not guilty. Through our investigators, we have found some of the witnesses who were genuinely with Dusko Tadic at the time these crimes were committed. You will hear how Dusko Tadic avoided his military draft. You will hear how he escaped from his home in Kozarac before 24th May with his wife and family to stay in the relative safety of Banja Luka. You will hear how the following month he secured a job in the traffic police of Prijedor, and you will hear how he worked every day in regular shifts together with others. You will hear how he then became involved in the local commune whose task was assisting refugees and attempting to rebuild the town of Kozarac. This evidence, your Honours, will be given to you by ordinary people, those who worked with him, those who lived with him, those who could see how he spent his time during the period in which this trial is concerned. All this evidence will be supported by documentary evidence such as duty lists to support the evidence given by witnesses for Dusko Tadic's position in the reserve police. We will present evidence that Dusko Tadic lived as a normal man alive as possible under these difficult times, that he was on duty as a reserve policeman who was engaged in the rebuilding of his scattered community throughout the time. With regard to his community, the Defence will assert that Dusko Tadic played no part whatsoever in rounding up and attacks on civilians. Naturally, the Prosecution will say that this alibi does not account for every minute of Dusko Tadic's time between May and December 1992; our answer to this is that no alibi could. To find an alibi to cover a period of eight months is a difficult matter, but the Defence is convinced that once the court has heard the accounts we will present of what Dusko Tadic was really doing during these months, you will see that we have provided impressive evidence to account for the whereabouts of Dusko Tadic during this period. The second limb of our defence will be the evidence of witnesses who will testify as to the kind of person Dusko Tadic was. Here they will tell you he was a man who had lived all his life in a Muslim community -- one of few Serbs in a town with a population of some thousands -- a man, they will tell you, who had many Muslim friends and who was distressed when people on both sides started displaying nationalistic tendencies and shunning their former friends. The Prosecution attempts to explain the fact that there is no evidence of any animosity shown by Dusko Tadic to Muslim people before the conflict by suggesting that he was some kind of spy or even fifth columnist. This, your Honours, is a feeble smoke screen to cover the deficiencies in their case. Many of his countrymen, though, see Dusko Tadic as a deserter who refused to fight for his country, and who left his village when the going got tough. The third limb of the defence is the evidence of those who were involved in these camps and who can testify that Dusko Tadic was not and could not have been there. It is not hard to imagine why it has been difficult for the Defence to obtain statements from people in this regard. These are people who, whether or not they had any personal involvement in the crimes that took place, are fearful for their own security, both from the prosecution by this Tribunal and from reprisals at home if they give evidence on matters which the authorities in the area wish to keep silent. Through these witnesses, your Honours, the Defence can present you with evidence which, we believe, will convince you that although these camps existed, although they were places in which unspeakable crimes occurred, these crimes were not and could not have been committed by the defendant. It is not the responsibility of the Defence to contest the political agenda of those who controlled the Opstina of Prijedor. Your Honours, I told you of the problems under which the Defence has laboured in order that the realities of the situation in the Opstina Prijedor are clearly before you. If you have at any time any problems arising from the Defence, you should resolve them by remembering that for every witness we produce for you at this trial, we could tell you of another 10 who could not or would not talk to us. In addition to the factual evidence we will put forward, the Defence will present you with evidence to support its view of the character of the conflict. Your Honours, I have come to the end of the opening statement of the Defence. We have informed you of our grave concerns about the proceedings of this trial. There are many problems which have not been solved and, unfortunately, there are many indications that these problems will not be solved. We are, therefore, deeply concerned about the quality of this trial. We fear that eventually it will not meet the demands for justice. We are standing, your Honours, on the edge of a fair trial. Do not push us over that edge. Help us to stay on the right side and to put forward our case. If you enable us, if you enable our witnesses to testify, you will not convict Dusko Tadic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wladimiroff. Mr. Niemann, are you ready to present your first witness? I understand it is Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am ready.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, then would you present your first witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. I call Dr. Gow. DR. JAMES GOW, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you stand there, please? There should be an oath in front of you. I will ask that you, please, take that oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, are you a political scientist with the positions of Lecturer in the Department of War Studies, Kings College, London, and a Research Associate of the Centre for Defence Studies in the University of London?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Formerly, were you a Research Officer at the Centre for Defence Studies and before that a lecturer on Soviet and Eastern European Affairs at the Hatfield Polytechnic in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt, if I may, for one moment. Would you state your full name, please, just for the record, unless I missed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Andrew James William Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I am sorry, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you hold the Degree of PhD, Doctor of Philosophy, from the University of London where you prepared your doctorial thesis on Yugoslavia at the School of Slavonic Studies and Eastern European studies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For the past several years has your work been concentrated on former Yugoslavia, particularly its military political affairs, and have you written and lectured extensively about this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your evidence based upon your personal knowledge and drawn from your own work and that of other recognised scholars in this field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you published reports, military and civilian writings, speeches and other official documents from the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have used documents of those kinds in preparing evidence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you have a knowledge of the relevant Yugoslav languages or the languages used in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have some knowledge of Serbo-Croat and some knowledge of Slovene.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you based your -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am finding it very hard to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I would wonder if the witness could speak up?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could you please raise your voice so that you are heard.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The microphone is helpful, but it does not really help us too much in the courtroom, so you really have to raise your voice even though you are speaking in the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, have you based your research on conversations with knowledgeable persons and witness statements and documents, some of which were made available to you by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Since 1988 have you published numerous books and articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are the details of those books, monographs, articles and other writings that you have published been presented in a schedule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would ask now that there be displayed on the computer screen the computer reference 1/1 to 1/4. If your Honours please, as promised, I have prepared for my friends in the Defence and for your Honours a copy of an index of the documents that will be used and referred to by Dr. Gow which may assist in following the exhibits as they are referred to. If I may, I hand those documents. (Handed)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, now what we are receiving is an index to the documents that Dr. Gow will be using?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am wearing glasses. They are relatively new glasses. I am still having difficulty seeing the print on this monitor. Is it possible that we could generate a hard copy of these at this time or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand at a subsequent time, but we may be able to have it slightly increased in size.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That looks better, thank you. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, just looking at the document that now appears on your screen -- I would ask that this document be scrolled through starting from the first page of it and slowly looking at it as we go through but in enlarged form -- when you look at that, is this the schedule that you just referred to a moment ago in your evidence relating to the articles that you have published and other writings in relation to former Yugoslavia? Perhaps you might do it a little more slowly, please? Dr. Gow, could you just acknowledge that as we progress through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This looks like the schedule to which I have just made reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is this the final page of the schedule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid at the moment I do not see the schedule so ..... Yes, excuse me, I had the wrong screen on.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I think you are asking the same thing that we are asking for. We are asking for a hard copy of this document. This has been marked for identification purposes as exhibit 1, I gather?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we will be seeking to tender.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does the Defence have a hard copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you need one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour, this is not quite disturbing in terms we need to read every word of it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Very good. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honours, I can produce a hard copy after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, are you looking at the final page of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does that refer to places where you have, in fact, delivered lectures from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour, and give the undertaking that I will provide a hard copy of the original.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 1 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, concerning the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia prior to 1991, can you tell the court about the political composition of that federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia comprised six republics and two autonomous provinces within the Republic of Serbia. The Republic of Serbia was the largest of the six republics. The others were Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the course of my opening this morning, your Honours, I showed you a document which I will now ask Dr. Gow to look at. Might the document No. 2 be shown on the screen, 2-1? (To the witness): Dr. Gow, is that a map of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map of the territories of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia showing the boundaries of the republics and the boundaries of the two autonomous provinces within Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this map prepared under your instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was prepared at my instruction by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender that map.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Noun whatsoever, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 2 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, could you tell the Trial Chamber of the ethnic composition of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, if I may, SFRY, was a complex mixture of populations. The largest groups were the Serbs, the Croats, the Slovenes, Macedonians and the Bosnian Muslims. There were a number of smaller groups usually classified as minorities, including Hungarians, Slovaks, a series of others, Vlahs, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you look at the map that will now be displayed on your monitor, 2/2? Dr. Gow, what is this a map of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map showing the territories of the former SFRY, as was, and on it is indicated the single largest ethnic group in any particular area across the territories of the republics of the SFRY. As indicating the single largest group, it does not necessarily indicate an absolute majority, but simply the single largest group within any particular area. Many parts of the territories of the SFRY had very mixed populations, particularly in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so where it shows, where the colour, for example, the blue indicates in this case the presence, for example, of Muslim populations in Bosnia, that does not mean that the Muslims were the absolute majority necessarily in those areas, and the same for the other colour codings in the scheme.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, at whose direction was this particular map prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map was prepared at my direction. It was prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From what was it compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was compiled from information derived from the 1981 census taken throughout the territories of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that map, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 3 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the computer document 1/5 be now brought up on the screen, please? (To the witness): Dr. Gow, I would ask you to look at your monitor now. You see that document, Dr. Gow? Can you tell me what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a schedule indicating the share within the total population of the SFRY of each of the main ethnic groups within the former Yugoslavia. The first column is based on the figures from the 1981 census; the second is based on the 1991 census. You will see that for the most part there is broadly no change in the period of 10 years, although I believe if you do scroll down towards the bottom you will see that there was a noticeable increase in the share of the proportion of Albanians within the total population of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At whose direction was this document prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document was prepared at my direction by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From what was it compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was compiled from the results of the 1981 and 1991 censuses in the SFRY and was derived in this particular form from minutes of evidence submitted to the House of Commons, Foreign Affairs Committee, in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 4 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, was any ethnic group wholly contained in any one republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SFRY was comprised of the six republics in the various communities. No group was entirely contained within one single republic of the SFRY, although the Republic of Slovenia was by far and away the most homogeneous ethnically of the republics with something around 90 per cent of the population being Slovene. In the other republics, in Serbia, around two-thirds of the population were Serbs; in Croatia, around three-quarters of the population were Croats; in Bosnia, the share was around 44 per cent Muslims, 30 or so, 33 per cent Serbs, 17 per cent Croats. So you see that no single ethnic group was contained within the boundaries of any one of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps in conjunction with that, might document 1-6 be put on the screen and perhaps the second half of that document might now be shown? Going back to the first half, Dr. Gow, just looking at the document on your screen, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document shows the percentage share of the population within each of the republics of the single largest group in that republic on the basis of data from the 1981 census. So you will see the first indications, the Republic of Slovenia was 90.5 per cent Slovene, reflecting, I think, the statement that I gave before; three-quarters of the population of Croatia were Croats; if you move down to the lower part of the schedule, you will see that around two-thirds of the total population of Serbia were Serbs, but, of course, you will note that if Serbia, taken without the two autonomous provinces, is looked at, the proportion rises to 85.4 per cent. The figures I indicated, around 44 per cent of the share of the Bosnian population were Muslims; that would be according to the 1991 census data, but here on the 1991 data it was around 39.2 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, Dr. Gow, was this document prepared at your direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 5 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, I would ask you now to look at the document that will be displayed on your monitor. Might document computer No. 1-7 to 1-8 be displayed? Just holding it there for a moment. Dr. Gow, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a copy taken from the minutes of evidence of the Foreign Affairs Committee Report in November, I think in November 1991. I made reference to it earlier in saying that some of the information in the schedules was derived from this source.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps the second half of the document could be now displayed for the sake of completeness? Are these the schedules which you relied on when you prepared the reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you scroll through, please, to the next part of the document? Yes. I tender that document, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is listed as 1/7-1/8. Will that become Exhibit 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 6, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Should I refer to it as Exhibit 6 being admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the better reference, your Honours. Perhaps I might just assist your Honour there; the numbers there are computer numbers which, apparently, assists with them locating it within the computer. The numbers 1/7 to 1/8 indicates the number of pages.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Two pages, OK. Very good. These exhibits have been exchanged, that is, you have provided the Defence with all of these exhibits, of course?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Exhibit 6 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, did the 1991 census show the ethnic composition of the various republics in the Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: According to that census, what was the population of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The population of Bosnia and Herzegovina was a little over 4 million, I think about 4.1 million, and of that total population 44 per cent were Slav Muslims, 31 per cent were Bosnian Serbs, and around 17 per cent Bosnian Croats and there were small groups of others.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that according to this Exhibit that we are looking at? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where do you basically derive that sort of information from, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That information is derived from census returns. I am not sure if they are included in the schedule here -- maybe if we could scroll back, I could check -- but from other documents that we have. These are taken -- these figures seem to be purely for 1981. If you take the table -- I am not sure. There you have the comparative figures for the totals from 1991 with the reservation on the Albanians being expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is the table 2 that appears on the screen now; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It provides a date, 1981, at the top and then there is above 1981 a number in relation to the Serbs, that is 8.14, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the total number of Serbs within the territories of the SFRY, according to that 1981 census, and in the right-hand column you have the total figures for the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Expressed beside that is the percentage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then it goes down through the various national groups. Dr. Gow, what language or languages do the various ethnic groups speak in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The principal language spoken on the territories of the former Yugoslavia was known as Serbo-Croat, spoken by around 80 per cent of the population. Two related but separate Slavonic languages were spoken, Slovene by the Slovenes, Macedonian by the Macedonians. The Albanians in the southern parts of the country, particularly in Serbia, spoke Albanian and other groups, Hungarians, for example, would speak Hungarian, although many of them would also speak Serbo-Croat as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What, if any, are the regional variations in the languages of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although Serbo-Croat was regarded as a single language by philologists, there were variations between the eastern and western variants. For example, the Serbian part of the old Yugoslavia in the east would use the Cyrillic script, whereas the western variant in Croatia would use the Latin script; the Cyrillic script being like Russian or Bulgarian and the Latin script being like French or Italian, the kind of script that we would use in English. There were also slight regional variations in the way things were said and variations in vocabulary. This has led some people to argue for the existence of separate languages on a socio-linguistic language, I understand, although I am not an expert in linguistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Turning to the question of religion, Dr. Gow, were there any variations in the religious beliefs of the various ethnic groups in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were. The various groups were the Orthodox Church, the Serbian Orthodox Church, also later the Montenegrin and Macedonian Orthodox Churches, being again like the Greek Orthodox or Russian Orthodox Church but with its own prelate. The western territories, in Croatia and in Slovenia, Roman Catholicism was the dominant religion, and in some parts of the country, in southern Serbia, among the Albanians in the Kosovo province within Serbia and among the Slav Muslims in the border areas of Montenegro and Serbia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Islam was taken as the cultural and religious -- was the religious characteristic, the dominant religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, earlier in your evidence you spoke of the population distribution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Concentrating now more specifically on the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, are you aware of the variations in the population distribution of this republic since 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that there has been significant displacement of the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you just look for a moment for me, please, at the document that will now be displayed on the screen, 1-9, and perhaps the bottom half of that could be shown in large form? Dr. Gow, what is this particular document we are now looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a table which indicates the change in the population distribution within particular areas throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina since 1991. You will see in the left-hand column a series of regions indicated. In the second column, ethnicity is indicated. The third column shows the 1991 census figures for each group, ethnic group, within those particular regions. The final column shows the figures in 1994 for the ethnic share within a particular region, and those figures are derived, the 1994 figures are derived, from UNHCR reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At whose direction was this document prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document was prepared at my direction by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will just look at the bottom section of that document now, if we could? Is any one particular region, the variation in numbers, more significant than others, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you will see that in a number of the regions there has been a significant change. If you look, for example, in the schedule, the part of the schedule that is being shown at the moment, second from the bottom is northern Bosnia and you will see that in that area there has been an increase of almost 100,000 of the Serb population in that area, but in the same time there has been a very significant decrease in the Croat and Muslim communities, the Croat community dropping, as you can see, from 180,000 to 30,000 and the Muslims in that area dropping from 355,000 to 40,000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to the Exhibit 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 7 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, would you look at the next document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: If I can ask a question? I am not quite clear how the census was taken in the troubled times of 1994 as, apparently, it was. Was it a complete census?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will direct the question to the witness about that, your Honour. I was about to move on to that, I think. Perhaps you heard what His Honour has said, can you assist us in how those figures were derived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may clarify, I believe I already said, but to be very clear, the 1994 figures are derived from UNHCR reports, not from censuses being taken. So, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, the agents in the area all working with the communities and designating the number of people from each community they were working with. This is not a census taken by State authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think following on from that, Dr. Gow, could you look at the next document which is shown on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I just follow up because the pre-war column on Exhibit 7, you indicated, was 1991. I gather that was an official census?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the official census taken by the Federal Statistical Office in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the next document be shown, 1-10 to 1-11, and could the front page of that be expanded? Dr. Gow, firstly, just looking at the front page of the document you see now on the screen, can you tell the Chamber what the document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a document produced by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and it is the kind of information that they produce from time to time to inform people of their activities and of the situation in areas where they are operating. This particular one is information on former Yugoslavia from September 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it related to the previous exhibit that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information which we were just discussing on the basis of the share of communities in particular regions was derived from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might go to the second page of this particular document, 1/11? Dr. Gow, are these the population estimate variations which you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 8 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, would you please look at the next document that I have displayed on the screen, document 2/3. What is that a map of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a map which indicates the directions in which large numbers of people took flight from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the course of 1992, you will see, going into the neighbouring states, into Croatia, into Montenegro and into Serbia. The bulk of those people, displaced people, were in three categories; those who were displaced within Bosnia, those who moved into neighbouring states and those who went into states further afield in western Europe and around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say it indicates that, is that indicated by the arrow that appears there, various arrows, that you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What does the green section that is highlighted there indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The green section highlighted indicates areas under Serbian control at that time within the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, was this particular map prepared under your direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map was prepared at my direction by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From what did you compile the information which you put on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information was derived again from the UNHCR reports to which I made reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection with respect to 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask you just a question with respect to 9? 9 will be admitted. There is no arrow, I gather, coming from Prijedor, is that correct, unless I am to consider that the arrow to the right would include Prijedor? I am sorry, Dr. Gow, help me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are correct to say that there is no arrow coming directly from Prijedor. The arrows are meant to be indicative only; they are not giving specific relation to any individual location, and people from Prijedor were, indeed, moving out northwards into Croatia as the arrow a little bit to the right would indicate. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, is there an electronic pencil there that, perhaps, you might be able to assist Her Honour by referring to things on the side of the computer? Perhaps you might just indicate where the people of Prijedor generally would have moved out of the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I am able to say, the people from Prijedor -- Prijedor is there -- would have been moving northwards into Croatia. Many of them also moved, I believe, westwards toward the Bihac area which had a predominantly Muslim population, and which remained that way throughout most of the war. I hope my little arrows are of some clarification. If not .....

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So they would have moved -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So people would be moving for the most part in those directions, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Who were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These predominantly would be Slav Muslims who were the largest group to move out of that area, as was indicated by my reference to the schedule area earlier on. It would be unfair to say that only Slav Muslims were moving from this area. People in all areas -- there were people of all communities being displaced in most areas. The difference is the numbers involved and the scale.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would like you now, please, if you would, to return to the historical political background of the former Yugoslavia. When was the entity known as Yugoslavia first proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was proclaimed on 1st December 1918.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I now wish to take you through a series of documents, a series of maps, in connection with the development of the Federal State of Yugoslavia. The first document I would ask you to look at is document 2-4, if you would, please? Dr. Gow, firstly, what is this a map of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map showing the territories which went to make up the kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes when it was formed on 1st December 1918, although I should also point out that that formation was not formally consolidated for another three years. If you read the map, you are able to see the evolution of the kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later renamed Yugoslavia. If I may try to make use of this gadgetry: First, there was roughly for most of a period of 500 years a dividing line between two empires which I will broadly indicate there. To the west and north was the Austro-Hungarian Hapsburg Empire; to the east and the south was the Ottoman (Turkish) Empire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may continue, but I was being beaten by the gadgetry. Thank you. In the course of the 19th century, there were some changes. First, the border between the two Empires moved from being the border between -- along the River Drina between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia indicated there, broadly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might show us again on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The River Drina, you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here. The border changed from being roughly the border between the River Drina forming the border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina to being the borders between Bosnia and Herzegovina and present-day Croatia. In 1878, Austria took up occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and so, therefore, it was transferred from what formally in 1908, but de facto in 1878, from one Empire to the other. In the course of the 19th century, Serbia began to become independent from the Turkish Ottoman Empire. Serbia, you see, the coloured areas indicated on the right-hand side of the map. Between 1814 and 1878, narrow Serbia, indicated by the darker green and by the line I am now trying to draw, became independent de facto in 1878 wholly from the Ottoman Empire. In the course of the Balkan Wars of 1911 to 1913, the territory of Serbia expanded to include the areas which now form Kosovo and Macedonia to the south and west and at the same time the area of Montenegro which had been independent more or less throughout the whole of this period also expanded to form a common border with Serbia. Those were the territories which went to make up the kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes when it was proclaimed in 1918.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this map prepared under your direction and supervision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender this map.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 10 will be admitted. Perhaps now would be a good time for us to take a recess. We will stand in recess until 4 o'clock. (3.20 p.m.) (The court adjourned for a short time) (4.00 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before Dr. Gow begins again, we were discussing how we might handle some of the exhibits, particularly the exhibits that Dr. Gow puts markings on. I understand that with our technological system that when the markings are put on they can be made permanent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, in some instances, the Judges are interested in having those exhibits on which there has been a marking made, made an additional exhibit. So, for example, the one where Dr. Gow drew the arrows reflecting where persons went from Prijedor, that was Exhibit 5, was it -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Exhibit 9, I think, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, map of routes. That was one that was helpful to us. So could you then make that the one with the markings 9A or how would you suggest it be handled?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours have no objection, I think probably the easiest way is to make it part of the exhibit, if that is OK, and we call it just part of Exhibit 9. What I will do now is that every time Dr. Gow makes a marking, I just have to request the technician people to make a copy of that and incorporate it as part of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The only possible objection -- I do not know; I will hear from the Defence -- is that you have received a copy of Exhibit 9 and I am sure you have discussed that and perhaps you may not have any objection. But now once there has been marking on Exhibit 9, you have not had an opportunity to cross-examine as to that. Would you have any objection to it coming in as 9 and then you would deal with the cross-examination later or how?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So far we have no problem with that, so we will not object to it. It may change during the process of examination, but so far there is no problem here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. So we will handle it -- if there is no objection to the modification that has been made of the exhibit, we will keep the same number, in this instance, it is 9, and that 9 will have the markings of Dr. Gow. If there is an objection made to the markings, then you will have to give it a different number ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Different number.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- perhaps and I do not know how we will handle the "a".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps, your Honours, just when thinking about it for a moment, though, it may be better if I give them an alphabetical number so every time there is a document that is marked, make it 9A, 9B and 9C, and that way it will be reflected in the transcript as well. The document can be marked that way. It might be easier.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think so. So 9 then will be the original map of the routes of population. The marking then would be 9A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We join in that idea; we think it is very practical indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. So now what we have admitted is 9, it is listed as 2/3 on your list; then we have 9A which would be the 9 with the markings of Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I might just, if I may, go back to Exhibit 9 and ask Dr. Gow to do it again and request that it be marked by him.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. I think there was one other exhibit that the Judges were considering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That was 11 -- no, 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Exhibit 10, the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will go to back.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So we will start back at 9 and let us create 9A and then 10, we are also interested in the markings being made a part of a separate exhibit. Fine. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, just looking at Exhibit 9A, I should say 9, looking at Exhibit 9 now displayed on your screen, would you please with the electronic pen mark there, as you did earlier in your evidence, the general directions or routes that were followed by people that were refugees from the Prijedor region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, I will mark Prijedor again for the record. I will give a general indication of directions which people may have taken. I would stress that all of this is not a matter of individual documentary record; it is simply a matter of general movements. Without wishing to pre-empt anything else, I would point out that in a number of cases they were given a certain kind of assistance to make these movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honours, and might a hard copy be made and it be given the number Exhibit 9A?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 9A?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Exhibit 9A will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, could you look at the next document that I show you, Exhibit 10? Dr. Gow, looking at that exhibit that you see there now, earlier on in your evidence you have made some markings on the exhibits in relation to division of the two Empires, the Austro-Hungarian Empire and the Ottoman Empire. Would you mind doing that again for us on a copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suggested that, among other places, the border between the two Empires -- maybe if I try some kind of shading here down here, along the River Drina, the border between Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina formed the border between the two Empires for the greater part of a period of 500 years, 400 or 500 years. But, in 1878, under the auspices of the Congress of Berlin, Austria annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina, so the border between two Empires de facto became this border here, the border between present-day Bosnia and present-day Croatia. That border was confirmed in 1908 when Bosnia and Herzegovina was fully transferred legally to the Austro-Hungarian Empire just following the de facto annexation in 1878.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, do you think, if the technology permits it, could you just write in the date against the two lines which might assist in separating them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try. I am afraid this is not so easy! Here was -- it is like being back at school, infants school. I hope that will clear it up for your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would ask that that be tendered as Exhibit 10(A).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 10A will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, while that exhibit is on the screen, is there anything else that you wish to draw our attention to in relation to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might clear the screen, so that if you are going to mark it again we can make it 10B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the recess, I was indicating the way in which during the course of the 19th century Serbia gained independence, first of all, in the area of narrow Serbia -- of narrow Serbia, the dark olivey green area marked on this map. If I could ask for some technical assistance? I keep trying to get the maker for the line and the screen rolls up. I have it now, thank you. The line marked by the dark olivey green on which "Serbia" is written, this was the line of Serbia as it became independent between 1814 and 1878. Independence was confirmed in 1878. I went on to say that in the course of the Balkan Wars between 1911 and 12, the territory of that independent Serbian state was expanded to include the territories marked in the buff colour, most of which today form the areas of Kosovo and Macedonia.
